Dear Brothers and Sisters,

Responding to the invitation of Mother Rita Caiaffa and of the Religious Institute Daughters of Saint Anne, the Charismatic Family Team would also like to propose a journey of celebrations, so that all of us may join in the Grateful Remembrance of these 160 years of the shared gift: the generous and fruitful “Yes” of our Blessed Mother Rosa.

“Remembering the past gives momentum to tomorrow and opens new horizons; therefore, celebrating the 160th anniversary of the Foundation [of the Religious Institute Daughters of Saint Anne] is not a point of arrival, but a point of departure, a renewed impetus; it is a confirmation that the values that have shaped us since 1866 are still alive and fruitful […] Contemplating this stretch of history, our gratitude to the Lord for the wonders He has accomplished flows forth spontaneously.”1

In this regard, our suggestion is to retrace the path that the Lord traced for Mother Rosa and, through her, for the entire Family of Saint Anne. With a very simple idea that can be used as Monthly Retreats, community, personal, and/or group reflections, according to need. Furthermore, in harmony with this proposal, it would be very appropriate to revisit the Catechesis of Pope Leo XIV for this year, which commemorates the Second Vatican Council.

Keeping in mind the proposed objective, we can adapt these materials to our own context, simplifying or enriching them according to concrete situations. The main purpose is to continue nurturing and keeping alive the beautiful experience of communion that has already been established among us.

Wishing everyone a fruitful journey, we offer our special congratulations to the religious Daughters of Saint Anne on their particular anniversary.

The Charismatic Family Team.

* For the common celebration, the following outline is proposed:

  1. Introduction:

For each celebration, an introduction is proposed according to the theme to be presented. However, since each charismatic expression uses the material according to its own context, a prior reading is necessary for the required adaptations.

  1. Opening prayer:

Prepare for reflection with a prayer or a hymn invoking the Holy Spirit and then recite together the prayer of Grateful Remembrance (cf. the last page).

  1. Listening to the Word:

A biblical text is proposed to enlighten and broaden the horizon of the reflection.

  1. Listening to Mother Rosa:

In addition to the biblical text, we propose the meditation of a passage from the writings of Mother Rosa to help deepen the theme presented.

  1. Commentary:

This brief reflection is intended as an aid for meditating on the proposed theme. However, nothing prevents giving space to one’s own creativity.

  1. Sharing / Deepening:

At this point, articles from our documents are proposed (each expression will refer to its own), along with questions to encourage sharing.

  1. Conclusion / Thanksgiving:

It is suggested to conclude with an appropriate prayer and hymn.

Father of eternal mercy, who in your infinite goodness inspired Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno to give life to the Institute of the “Daughters of Saint Anne”, and through

them to all the different expressions of our Charism,

we give you thanks for this ineffable gift bestowed

upon the Church and the world.

To you be our praise for all the Sisters who, following the inspiration of Blessed Mother Rosa, have lived with great fidelity throughout these 160 years and have collaborated in the Church and with the Church in the saving work of Christ.

Help us to live in creative fidelity to our common Charism, docile to the promptings of the Holy Spirit and open to the signs of the times and places. May we, together with the members of the great Family of Saint Anne, live in a true spirit of family and, with all our other brothers and sisters,

in maternal and paternal dedication.

May our glorious Mother Saint Anne take us by the hand and shape our lives according to her virtues, so that we may live true poverty of heart, seeking nothing on this earth but the Lord. Amen!

Introduction

Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno entrusted to her “Memorie” the description of a vision concerning “the three drops of blood that were to be the three Orders” which the Lord was asking her to found (cf. Mem., p. 624). Yet, whenever she mentions it, she does not specify the date or circumstances, since, for her at that time, everything was still unclear and undefined.

With these “three drops of blood”, Mother Rosa certainly refers to a vision she had in the past, most likely even before the foundation of the Daughters of Saint Anne, and which she interpreted as a sign pointing to multiple foundations. Thus, in this “vision” we glimpse the inspiration of a great and beautiful Family:

“Remember the three drops of my blood that I showed you

and that I poured upon your heart; I told you that they would be the three

Orders that you were to [found].” (Memorie, p. 665)

From this inspiration, for more than 40 years, the Family of Saint Anne has been nurturing relationships marked by communion and complementarity. In the “family spirit” that unites us, we share the gifts of different vocations which, in fidelity to the common Charism, “collaborate in the Church and with the Church in the saving work of Christ”.

Invocation to the Holy Spirit

  • Begin the meeting/reflection with a prayer or a hymn invoking the Holy Spirit and then recite the prayer of grateful remembrance (cf. introduction).

  • Then read the proposed biblical text and the passage taken from the writings of Mother Rosa, followed by the reflection.

  • Pause each moment with periods of silence…

From the Book of Proverbs

(2:1-15)

My son, if you accept my words and store up my commands within you, turning your ear to wisdom and applying your heart to understanding; indeed, if you call out for insight and cry aloud for understanding, and if you look for it as for silver and search for it as for hidden treasure, then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God. For the Lord gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and prudence. He holds success in store for the upright, he is a shield to those whose walk is blameless, for he guards the course of the just and protects the way of his faithful ones. Then you will understand what is right and just and fair—every good path. For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul. Discretion will protect you, and understanding will guard you, saving you from the way of evil, from those whose words are perverse, who have left the straight paths to walk in dark ways, who delight in doing wrong and rejoice in the perverseness of evil, whose paths are crooked and whose ways are devious.

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, pp. 624 and 665)

“The three drops of blood that were to be the three Orders are always before me. I had never thought of the Sons of Saint Anne, but believed it should be a branch of the Daughters of Saint Anne with a contemplative, cloistered life. Instead, the Sons and the Tertiaries of Saint Anne. Oh my Mother!

— Remember the three drops of my blood that I showed you and that I poured upon your heart; I told you that they would be the three Orders that you were to [found]. — Oh my Love, how can this be - I say within myself - I who am so old, how will I manage? I am full of suffering, ill, and I feel that I cannot go on. It is true that you make the dead live and the dying work, for I can say that my suffering is a daily agony; I do not speak of the pains, for that would require too much time.”

At first, the real meaning symbolised by the “three drops of blood” shown to her in a vision from the past was not clear. Little by little, Mother Rosa received further light regarding the “three Orders” that God wanted her to found.

  • The 1st drop – The Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne:

On a night of intense prayer before her “Crucified Beloved” (in February 1864), Mother Rosa received from the Lord the inspiration for the first foundation: the Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne:

“When [the prayer] ended, I felt so beside myself. I put everything away and then, taking my dear Crucifix again, I thanked him. Oh, how I pressed my Love to my breast! Having said this, I was once again rapt in ecstasy, and I clearly felt that he himself was dictating a Rule to me. Thus he spoke to me, and what he dictated was so clear; it seemed that this dictation produced in me a different effect.

— Write at once what I have told you.

These were the last words, and when I came to myself, I did not delay in obeying. I wrote down exactly what he had dictated to me and carefully preserved it.” (Memorie, p. 256)

Advised by her Confessor and by the Bishop, she resisted this call for a long time, but two years later she yielded before the authoritative and firm invitation of the Holy Father Pius IX, who ordered her (January 3, 1866) to begin the foundation at once. About two months later, on March 13, 1866, she left Genoa for Piacenza with her first five companions to begin God’s work.

  • The 2nd drop – The Third Order of Saint Anne:

The second drop was always somewhat “controversial” for Mother Rosa. At first she thought it referred to the work she was preparing to found in collaboration with the Bishop of Piacenza, Msgr. Giovanni Battista Scalabrini: an Institute for deaf-mute girls, called the “Tertiaries of Saint Anne”. Yet the “doubt” remained:

“I fear that it is not God’s will that I occupy myself with the ‘Third Order of Saint Anne.’ [This situation] is harder than death. […] The work of the Tertiaries, and moreover joined together with the Bishop? This will not be it, but rather something else [for which] it will be necessary to struggle.” (Memorie, p. 664)

Only through the “Deposition of Princess Emilia of Fitalia” (in the Roman Process for the Cause of Canonisation of Mother Rosa – Session 319, p. 2451v) do we learn of her intention to found the “Third Order of Saint Anne”, with an organisation and juridical form quite different:

“However, when Mother Gattorno was about to come to Palermo, Sister Anna del Salvatore spoke to me about her with great enthusiasm, wishing that I too might meet her. Upon her arrival, she herself introduced me to the servant of God. […] Our conversation (which was also the only one during that first visit to Sicily) revolved around a project of hers to found a Third Order of the Daughters of Saint Anne; a project that would also extend to men. She promised me, of her own accord, that she would enroll me in this Third Order, as well as my husband...” (Positio super virtutibus, p. 427)

This project, as it was configured, brings us today to what we know as the “Movement of Hope”:

The ‘Movement of Hope,’ named as such starting May 24, 1989, is rooted in the inspiration of Mother Rosa Gattorno, who tried on multiple occasions to organise it in a juridical form without success; […] it regained momentum, gradually defining itself more clearly, constituting itself as a Movement, based on the intuition of Rita Di Maggio, who, during the solemn celebration of December 9, 1981, on the occasion of the translation of the venerated mortal remains of Blessed Rosa Gattorno from the General House to the Church of Sant’Anna at the Lateran, felt the impulse to spread Mother Rosa’s charism among the laity.” (Statute of the Movement of Hope, art. 1)

The approval by the Ecclesiastical Authority firmly places the Movement within the life and holiness of the Church, as well as within the Charismatic Family of Saint Anne (cf. Statute of the Movement of Hope, art. 13).

  • The 3rd drop – The Religious Institute of the Sons of Saint Anne:

In the same pages where she recounts the vision of the “three drops of blood”, on December 29, 1882, she recounts for the first time the intuition to also found the Sons of Saint Anne:

“…Thus [regarding] the matter of the foundation of the Sons of Saint Anne; it was so clearly shown to me that it was God’s will that I go to the Pope and tell him everything that God had suggested to me and not delay in obeying […]; Oh my Love, what a second piercing! Not yet healed from the first wound, you wish to open another sore; may your holy will be done in all things.” (Memorie, p. 623)

By 1886, the project seemed to take a clearer shape, and the intimate inspiration was repeatedly confirmed by divine intervention. Yet, years of uncertainties, fears, and difficulties followed. For many vicissitudes, Mother Rosa felt that the project, as it was being configured, was not yet what God desired. Sustained by the certainty that, at the right moment, God’s hour would strike also for the “Sons of Saint Anne”, Mother Rosa entrusted the realisation of this singular design to Divine Providence.

  • Further inspiration of Mother Rosa: Contemplative Daughters of Saint Anne Perpetual Adorers

In her autobiographical accounts, Mother Rosa recounts a further vision granted to her by Fr. Bernardo concerning “another new foundation of cloistered nuns”. Therefore, when she wrote about the vision of the “three drops,” she thought that this might be one of the “three Orders” she was to found: “But I believed it was to be the branch of the Daughters of Saint Anne devoted to contemplative, cloistered life!” (Memoirs, p. 624). Most likely, she thought the same in 1884, when the community of the “Tertiaries of Saint Anne, Perpetual Adorers of the Most Blessed Sacrament” began.

Yet, what Mother Rosa had glimpsed when she spoke of the Daughters of Saint Anne dedicated to contemplative, cloistered life would be more fully set out in the “Rule” she wrote in 1891, which makes the further inspiration behind this foundation quite clear.

  • Inspired by Mother Rosa: Secular Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne

As early as 1986, inspired by the newness brought about by the Second Vatican Council, Francisca Adália de Oliveira Tavares, together with a group of young women, began a new path of sanctification, re-proposing within consecrated secularity, the Charism of Mother Rosa and the distinctive spirituality of the Family of Saint Anne.

“Blessed Rosa Gattorno, under the action of the Holy Spirit, intuited this spirituality, and through the power of the same Spirit, Francisca Adália Tavares de Oliveira made this same gift concrete in the Secular Institute Daughters of Saint Anne.” (Constitutions of the Secular Institute Daughters of Saint Anne, art. 2)

Many “dreams” and projects were entrusted to Mother Rosa, which today we see happily realised in a “Single Charismatic Family”. But we must give thanks for the boldness of Mother A. Virginia Sinagra and many other Sisters, Daughters of Saint Anne, who were able to interpret the signs and perceive, over time and through history, God’s will for us.

To God, rich in mercy, who in Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno revealed the common Charism entrusted to us, we confidently offer our prayer:

R. Renew us, Lord, in your Holy Spirit.

  1. Lord, who gives us the joy of celebrating the glorious memory of Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno, grant that we may always rejoice in her maternal intercession. We pray. R.

  2. Lord, make our Charismatic Family a living and effective instrument in proclaiming Your Word, and, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, may we, in conformity with our spirituality, make Your merciful face known to the world. We pray. R.

  3. Lord, who gave us Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno as mother, founder, and inspirer, grant that we may place all our efforts in fostering unity among brothers and sisters, and in spreading her Charism. We pray. R.

Our Father

Almighty and eternal God, who granted your servant Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno the grace to conform to Christ poor and crucified, through ardent faith and admirable charity, grant that we, following her example, may work tirelessly for the good of the poor and humble. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, Your Son, who is God, and lives and reigns with You, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

Introduction

On a night of intense prayer before “Her Crucified Beloved” (the exact date is not specified, but it was in February 1864), Mother Rosa received from the Lord an inspiration whose meaning she did not at first understand.

In obedience, having been placed in charge of the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, whose director was Fr. Frassinetti, she was entrusted with revising the rules he had written for that Congregation so that they might obtain the Archbishop’s approval. Though fearing she was not capable of doing so, Mother Rosa agreed with simplicity and great humility.

In the silence of her room, where every evening she poured herself out in long prayers or in silent contemplation before her “Crucified Beloved”, unaware of what was about to happen, she prayed humbly: “My Love, if I must obey, then You inspire me […] show me where the difficulties to be removed are.” She reads and rereads, and light dawns in her mind: “The Archbishop is right; some modifications are necessary” (Memorie, p. 256). She underlines and writes with ease. When that task is finished, she resumes praying.

But an inner voice urges her to take up the pen again and continue writing. She obeys, wholly absorbed in her “Beloved”, and almost unaware of what she is doing. In the end, she understands clearly: it was the inspiration for a Rule for a new Institute - what would become her first foundation.

From the Letter of St Paul to Titus

(2:11-14)

My son, the grace of God has finally appeared, bringing salvation to all people and teaching us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live in this world with sobriety, justice, and piety, as we await the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ.

He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all iniquity and to form for Himself a pure people who belong to Him, full of zeal for good works.

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 256)

“Having arrived in my room, I placed these Rules at the feet of my dear Crucifix. [I said:] My Love, if I must obey, then You inspire me. And I thought no more about it. Late into the night, I took into my arms the dear Crucifix and the Rules: Tell me, my Love, where are the difficulties that must be removed?

Thus, in that position, I remained enraptured, and a voice told me what I had to remove, for the Archbishop was right not to approve [the Rules] with those principles, because it was not the will of God. When I came to myself, I kissed and thanked my Beloved; immediately I went to the table, leafed through that little booklet, and on a sheet of paper I wrote everything, precisely as my God had told me.

When I had finished, I felt so outside of myself; I folded everything, and then again, taking my dear Crucifix, I thanked Him. Oh, how I pressed my Love to my heart! Having said this, I found myself once more enraptured in ecstasy, and I clearly felt that He Himself was dictating a Rule to me. What He dictated was so clear; it seemed that a different effect was produced in me by this dictation.

— Write at once what I have told you.

These were the last words, and when I came to myself, I did not delay in obeying. I wrote down exactly what had been dictated to me and carefully put it away. I returned to prayer, and nothing troubled me.”

As we have been able to reflect more deeply, this Inspiration was not immediately clear to Mother Rosa. She had to receive further light, little by little, in order to understand the Will that the Lord was asking of her.

At first, without understanding, she gave it no thought. But suddenly she was seized by a strange feeling, like an inner impulse towards something that had to be done—unclear, yet necessary and urgent. She prayed, asking for light, and as this interior movement gradually took shape and became clearer, she felt terrified:

“Those [Rules] that I had put away began to trouble me, because an inner voice kept tormenting me, telling me that I had to show them, that it was His work. But I pushed [the thought] away and, to be more exact, I did not understand what was wanted.” (Memorie, p. 257)

She had to take up again the new sheet written that night and show it to her confessor and… no, those norms could not refer to an association of consecrated women in the world; it was something quite different:

“— What do You want, my dear Crucifix? Why must I show this writing? What is it for? He answered me:

— For the Work that I desire; it will be great!

My God! I began to think, but I understood nothing: where is this Work to be, and who is to carry it out? I felt so confused that I stopped thinking and began to pray, clinging to my dear Crucifix. A voice, which was certainly His, my Beloved’s, said to me:

— From you I want this Work; bring the writing you are holding to the Archbishop.” (Memorie, p. 257).

Her confessor reproached her for not having spoken of it immediately and ordered her to speak about it clearly to the Archbishop. The Archbishop, recognising in the sequence of events the sign of God’s will, clarified for her what she was to do.

“Oh, how my mind was troubled! Another Work? How can I undertake it? What shame to say this to the Archbishop! Oh, my God! I feel that my strength is not enough to do what You command me; I feel as though I am dying at the mere thought of it. And my children? My mother? And I wept. — No, my Jesus, I do not have the courage; I cannot!” (Ibidem).

Mother Rosa was truly overwhelmed. She saw the antithesis of her situation: the will of God calling her beyond the normal path of her natural duties as mother and daughter; an authoritative command that seemed, in itself, to oppose her fundamental obligations.

“As soon as [the draft of the Rule] was read, the Archbishop wrote to summon me to him. I cannot describe my confusion, my distress; I trembled like a leaf. I was so agitated that, once at his feet, there was no way for me to speak. He noticed my state and, knowing my disposition, merely told me to strive to carry out the Lord’s orders and assured me that the Work would certainly be very beautiful. It was only necessary to draft an internal regulation on top of it. I, confused, responded to everything with ‘yes’.” (Ibidem).

She took time, cried, and prayed intensely. Yet, in her painful perplexity, with the insistence of her confessor and the Archbishop, she became convinced that she must obey. She spoke with a few of her closest friends who might help her in the Foundation. In asking, she secretly hoped for a refusal, hoped for some obstacle, yet she could not close her heart to the inner compulsion. After a few months, she found five of her friends willing to follow her.

To accomplish God’s will, Mother Rosa had to face extremely difficult trials, endure deep humiliations, and bear unspeakable pains. For this reason, in her account, she cannot separate the historical events from her personal experience of faith and love; she personalises everything, embodying it in her suffering or her joy, always in relation to the “Supreme Good”, living from her very life.

This account of the gestation of God’s Work, with its strongly autobiographical character, allows us to follow Mother Rosa in her first discovery of herself as Founder, guided by God, of a Work whose fundamental outlines she clearly perceives, while fully aware that accepting God’s plan would completely upheave her existence, beginning with the painful separation from her children and parents.

“I shared my doubts with him, saying that it could be a diabolical work, having two children and very old father and mother, to whom I was very attached, and that I could not do this, to leave them—no! And my children… the very thought of leaving them was agony, and I kept repeating to myself:

— No, it will never be, no!“ (Memorie, p. 259).

Having overcome human resistance, though not without tribulations, Mother Rosa fully embraced the will of her “Crucified Beloved”, initiating the Work of God, which she later named “Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate Mary”. Her doubts and uncertainties were no obstacle for God, who found in her a response of radical love. The same availability is now required of the entire Family that has arisen in the Church from her generous yes.

Introduction

From the heavy task to which she felt obliged, a spark of hope flashed in Mother Rosa’s heart: she would go to the Pope. Only he, with his Supreme authority, could free her from an unbearable situation. “Never again”, she said to herself, with renewed trust, “will the Pope allow a mother to leave her children. Ah no, my Love, You will not allow it! Your Vicar will give me peace and relief in such a cruel battle” (Memorie, p. 260).

With this new hope, she shared her plan with the Archbishop, who, moved by her distress, consented and gave her letters of recommendation for several Roman ecclesiastical figures. She also expressed to her family her desire to visit Rome, without revealing the true purpose of her journey, and her parents were greatly pleased. Mr. Gattorno booked their passage — hers and her companion’s — on one of the best steamships serving between Genoa and Livorno at that time; from Livorno they would then continue by train to Rome:

“We departed on the day before New Year’s Eve 1866, on December 28 of the year ending, 1865. I arrived in Rome after suffering terribly […]

we arrived at one o’clock on January 1, 1866. […] An audience was requested, which was granted on January 3 at five o’clock after lunch:

it was a private audience.” (Memorie, p. 260).

From the Letter to the Hebrews

(10:1-7)

For the Law, indeed, having only a shadow of the good things to come and not the reality of the things themselves, can never by the same sacrifices - repeated year after year - make perfect those who draw near to God. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, purified once for all, would have no more consciousness of sins? But in these sacrifices, the remembrance of sins is renewed year by year. Indeed, it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Therefore, when Christ came into the world, He said: “You did not desire sacrifice or offering, but a body You prepared for Me. You were not pleased with burnt offerings or sin offerings. Then I said: ‘Behold, I come - it is written of Me in the scroll of the book - to do, O God, Your will’.”

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 261)

“Oh, I shall never forget that day! My hopes vanished, and the most bitter knife came to wound me deeply. I had already presented to the Supreme Pontiff the Rules - those which my dear Crucified Beloved had dictated to me and which, according to the Holy Father, were like commandments. As soon as I was at his holy feet, Pius IX blessed me, and rising, holding my hand in his, he said that he had read those Rules, that they were truly beautiful, and that I must not delay in putting them into execution. Oh! I threw myself to the ground and, crying, said to him:

— Your Holiness, I have two children, an old father and mother; both of my children are very young! He answered me:

— It is of no use; God wills it so.

— Oh no, Your Holiness, God, according to the holy Gospel, will hold me accountable for my children! And I wept bitterly.

— I love them too much, I cannot leave them; Your Holiness, it is impossible!

The Holy Father paused and, in a severe tone, said to me:

— Well then, if you do not do what God wants from you, you will have remorse for all the days of your life; your conscience will torment you, and you will have no peace. I was frightened and replied:

— No, Your Holiness, I want to do the will of God.”

According to our shared purpose, today we want to focus on this statement of Mother Rosa: “Your Holiness, I want to do the will of God”, which resonates fully with what the author of the Letter to the Hebrews says: “Behold, I come, O God, to do Your will”.

By rereading this through the lens of sacrifice and offering, as understood in the Old Covenant, we see how Christ presents His life to the Father, showing us the true and only worship pleasing to God: the offering of oneself. In this way, we can understand with what spirit Mother Rosa, in her total self-oblation, presents to the Father her own “Here I am”.

“I rose, and I could hardly speak; I felt my heart breaking. He brought me to his desk and gave me two of his photographs, writing a motto on each. Oh, how I felt! Nothing comforted me!” (Memorie, p. 262)

Already informed of the purpose of the audience and the visitor’s circumstances, Pope Pius IX received Mother Rosa with particular kindness, listened attentively, but immediately put an end to her hopes, telling her that she must not delay in fulfilling the will of God.

From Mother Rosa’s heart burst the cry of maternal despair: “Your Holiness, I cannot abandon my children! God will hold me accountable!” But the Pope’s face grew serious: “If you do not do what God wants from you, you will be tormented your entire life, and you will have no peace!”

It was almost too much for Mother Rosa’s soul. Yet, in a surge where faith overwhelms every human feeling and reasoning, she promised: “Your Holiness, I want to do the will of God”. At these words, the Pope was moved, comforted her, assured her of his support, and above all, of divine assistance: “God will take care of your children; you take care of God in His Work.”

The author of the Letter to the Hebrews understood that with the Incarnation of the Word, a new way was offered to all who wish to respond to God’s call — to live faith in Him and to bear witness to charity towards others. This involves taking up again the prophetic line of the Old Testament to understand, in the light of Jesus’ Paschal Mystery, that we are called to offer our life and place our existence in God’s hands, so that it may be His sign and not a selfish pursuit of our own advantage.

Mother Rosa likewise recognised in the authoritative words of the Vicar of Christ the will of God. She did not resist. On the contrary, in a resolute manner, she responded: “Your Holiness, I want to do the will of God”. Here, we witness the dynamic of a gift that generates another gift.

Therefore, it is necessary that we enter into the dynamic of giving and receiving, offering our own story, the flesh that makes us who we are, the feelings we carry in our hearts. It is life itself that must be transformed into grace, revealing God’s benevolence, bearing witness to His primacy, and manifesting the gift of His presence.

From Mother Rosa, we have much to learn about this. In the gift she received, she had to offer her heart, her life, her children, her parents… all within the dynamic of Christ’s offering, which always marked her existence.

For this reason, we are all called to live the dynamic of giving ourselves even within religious and parish communities, which — like families — must be spaces of gratuitous gift received and of self-offering. This does not depend on the other’s ability to receive, but on my courage and my love in offering myself.

If this risk is not lived, if the offering does not involve me, if the gift I give does not flow from who I am, then Mother Rosa’s Yes, or the Incarnation itself, cannot serve as a model for our relationships, and the dynamic of this gift does not touch us.

By calling me to holiness, God asks me to live as He lives and gives me His Spirit so that I, in love, may recognise myself, as Mother Rosa did, as a gift and may give myself to others, who in turn are gifts for themselves and for me. Christ desires to live in the gift and knows that this is what the Father wants of Him: to become a transparency of His love for humanity, in the diverse possibilities that human nature allows.

Therefore, to say, like Mother Rosa, “I want to do the will of God” means that the gift received must be lived not according to human criteria, but in accordance with what the Lord desires, according to the will that determined the gift: “God will take care of everything […] nothing will be lacking to you; all will be given to you”.

Mother Rosa’s Yes, echoing the Yes of the divine Word in the Incarnation, carried such dynamic force that the Work she undertook continues even today to act through the generous yes of every member of her Charismatic Family.

Introduction

After leaving the private audience with the Holy Father, Pope Pius IX, with her heart in turmoil, Mother Rosa returned to her room and abandoned herself to weeping throughout the night. At daybreak, she hurried to the Church of San Marcello al Corso, and before the image of the Sorrowful Virgin, her own heart pierced as well, she poured out her lament: “I must abandon my children! Your Son, through His Vicar, commands me to do it! I feel torn apart by grief; I love them so deeply”.

After this outpouring, she fell silent and remained absorbed in prayer for a long time. It seemed to her that Mary, the Mother of Sorrows, spoke to her heart, assuring her that she herself would care for her children. Mother Rosa rose from prayer comforted, transformed, and ready, as she herself would say, “to make the sacrifice of Abraham”. A sacrifice that would last her entire life.

In memory of this act of trusting surrender at the feet of the Sorrowful Virgin, we too wish to renew not only our devotion but also our love for the Blessed Virgin Mary, for in her we see the living and concrete realisation of our ideal of life. Therefore, consistent with our spirituality and origins, we embrace the words of the liturgy: “Draw us to you, O Immaculate Virgin; we will follow after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (cf. Divine Office for the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception).

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 265)

“I went to the feet of the Sorrowful Virgin in the church of the Servites where, after the death of their father, I had brought my children. To her, Most Holy Virgin, I entrusted them in such a resolute way. It seemed to me that she herself would take full care of them, and an interior voice assured me of this. Prostrating myself at the feet of this sovereign Queen of Sorrows, in bitter tears I said to her:

— I must abandon my children! Your Son, through His Vicar, commands me to do so! I feel torn apart by grief; I love them so dearly! You, my Mother, experienced the abandonment of Jesus; what did it cost you even to lose Him for three days! Oh, my children! I do not know how to find peace. Leave them? And where? And with whom? Alas, this is too much! How unhappy I am! I am a mother and I love them so deeply! Mary, Mary, my Mother, what a knife this is — it pierces me to the marrow of my bones!

I remained absorbed in prayer; my tears dried, and in the Most Holy Virgin I found peace and strength. When I came to myself, I felt transformed, like a giant. With generosity I offered them to God and repeated to Him the words of Abraham: Here I am, to fulfil Your divine will. I no longer returned to complaints or insistent attempts to withdraw, nor to a thousand protests.

Having offered myself as a victim for His Work, I received very great consolations, and the Most Holy Virgin assured me that she would always be with me and that my children would be hers. Oh, sweet word! And so it was.”

United intimately with the work of her Son’s Salvation, Mary is venerated by Mother Rosa with particular love, since, present in the life and sacrifice of Christ, she continues to be present in its realisation in her own life:

“You, my Mother, experienced the abandonment of Jesus; what did it cost you even to lose Him for three days! Oh, my children! I do not know how to find peace. Leave them? And where? And with whom? Alas, this is too much!” (Memorie, p. 265)

The presence of Mary, the Mother, becomes a source of renewed energy, comfort, light, and strength in her offering. Supported and guided by her maternal presence and intercession, Mother Rosa grows in the certainty that she must offer herself for Jesus and for His Work. Mary’s illuminations, indications, and desires are the foundation of her adherence to God’s plan:

“I remained absorbed; my tears dried, and in the Most Holy Virgin I found peace and strength. When I came to myself, I felt transformed, like a giant. With generosity I offered them to God and repeated to Him the words of Abraham: ‘Here I am, to fulfil Your divine will.’ I no longer returned to complaints or insistent attempts to withdraw, nor to a thousand protests.” (Ibidem).

After purifying herself in her sorrow, Mother Rosa finds herself at Mary’s feet humbler, pacified, and free, enjoying the peace of the little ones. In this way, she enters fully into the mystery of Christ, the Poor One of the Father.

She learns from the Mother and the Son the path of trusting abandonment, of descent, of losing life in order to find it. She learns from Mary, associated with the life of the Son, to be attentive, delicate, to bring joy, and to give space to the humble and the poor, following the indications of God’s humbling, who delights in the absolute poverty and gratuity of Mary.

“Having offered myself as a victim for His Work, I received very great consolations, and the Most Holy Virgin assured me that she would always be with me and that my children would be hers!” (Ibidem).

In describing these events, where one perceives the passage from union with Mary to contemplation of Jesus, it is clear that conformity to Him happens through a participation that is both suffering and resolutely offered.

“Mary, Mary, my Mother, what a knife this is—it pierces me to the marrow of my bones! I remained absorbed; my tears dried, and in the Most Holy Virgin I found peace and strength.” (Ibidem).

The path to serenity and peace passes through this oblation at Mary’s feet. She, as Mother, is the tangible sign of God’s infinite mercy. From her, Mother Rosa receives as a gift the certainty that in weakness or tribulation, the strength of her maternal presence will always sustain her and her children.

The work God accomplished in Mary, associating her with the salvific mystery of the Son, has permanent value in Mother Rosa’s life. The efficacy of the Mother’s mission, for all time and for every person who allows herself to be guided docilely by her, is an experience that generates full adherence to God’s Economy, which sent the Son to bring it to fulfillment: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman”.

In its brevity, the passage from the Letter to the Galatians we have meditated on is the summary of this mystery. The Trinity is present: God the Father, His Son, and the Holy Spirit; the Incarnation: “God sent His Son”; all this not in abstraction or outside of time, but in a history of salvation: “when the fullness of time had come”. And the discreet but essential presence of Mary is also there: “born of a woman”. Finally, there is the fruit of all this: men and women made children of God and of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Introduction

On the return journey from Rome to Genoa, the priest who was accompanying her, Don Luigi Cogrossi, persuaded her to stop in Piacenza instead of taking the sea route again. In Piacenza, he told her, she would meet some good priests who could be of help to her.

“At last we decided to leave after 28 days of suffering […] While we were travelling [with] this friend of mine and a priest — whom I had also met in our same lodging and who came with us — since I was suffering greatly, they suggested that I stop in Piacenza, [where] there were two very good souls and I would make their acquaintance. I allowed myself to be persuaded, and we stopped at an inn. Shortly afterwards, these two priests of excellent spirit arrived, and I told them everything that had happened to me and the reason for my journey to Rome.” (Memorie, p. 266).

And Mother Rosa, surprisingly, allows herself to be convinced. It must be said that she must have found herself — as was only natural — in a very particular state of mind, while Cogrossi was astutely pursuing his personal aims; yet over everything and everyone, as always, Providence was at work.

From the Letter of St Paul to the Romans

(8, 28-32)

Brothers, we know that all things work together for the good of those who love God, of those who are called according to His purpose. For those whom He has loved from the beginning, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers. If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also give us everything else along with Him?

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 266)

“These good souls, having understood this, begged me to begin the Work in Piacenza. They pointed out to me that it was a peaceful city and that there was a good Bishop there who was very fond of good works; they themselves would gladly help and would look for a suitable place. No sooner said than done, they took care of finding a temporary apartment; later on, a palace would be purchased. I leave it to you to imagine how painful these plans were for me. I always thought that it would still take some time, when, just a few days after my return from Rome, I received a letter from these priests telling me that they had found the house and wanted an immediate reply.

Strengthened and having already made my offering, I replied that they should secure it, and that by the beginning of March I would go there with some of my friends — and so it happened.

My God, how was I to tell this to papa and mama? And to the Archbishop? In giving him the report of the journey and of the audience, I had not spoken to him at all about my stop in Piacenza, because I did not have the courage… I gathered my courage and told everything also to the Archbishop, who absolutely did not want me to leave Genoa and told me that he did not give his approval. My God, what was I to do? … Throwing myself to the ground at the feet of my Crucifix, I prayed: ‘Tell me, my Love, was this stop in Piacenza your work, or my illusion? Did I allow myself to be misled by those who advised me to do this? If I must not go, or whatever Your will may be, speak to me and I will carry out Your commands; but take me out of this fierce struggle and grant that my Archbishop may consent and bless me.’ A clear voice:

— ’It is entirely My will that this has happened; be at peace, everything will be made smooth.”

To the recurring and sometimes doubtful question of whether and how God takes care of us, the Word responds with luminous and solid certainty: “all things work together for the good of those who love God, of those who are called according to His purpose”.

With these concise words, we can also affirm the certainty of divine Providence in the choice to begin God’s Work in Piacenza, precisely because we find confirmation of it in revelation, which is richly expressed in the Memorie: “It is entirely My will that this has happened; be at peace, everything will be made smooth”.

The element of the Lord’s care, “He preserves the gift”, also seals Mother Rosa’s offering, to which she could respond: “I needed nothing else, and after thanking my dear Crucifix, full of trust, I prepared for departure” (Memorie, p. 268).

Humanly speaking, however, Mother Rosa, with the typically Genovese practicality she possessed in abundance, could not fail to understand that in Piacenza the Foundation would face not fewer but greater difficulties than in Genoa. Piacenza, only recently annexed to Piedmont, was completely unknown to her, just as she was entirely foreign and unknown in that city. In Genoa, she knew she could count not only on the Archbishop but also on many others who could provide valuable help.

Yet men are only instruments, often unaware, sometimes even opposed or contradictory, but always instruments in God’s plans. In any case, it was truly God’s plan that the new Work should begin precisely in Piacenza, even if difficulties and sufferings were never lacking.

I returned to Genoa at the beginning of February while Don Luigi stayed in Piacenza. There was great discontent from the Archbishop of Genoa when he learned of Mother Rosa’s decision, and only with great difficulty did she obtain his first approval and blessing. Her companions, however, were ready to follow her.

She still had to communicate her decision to her parents. It was an ordeal for them, and their grief moved and caused unspeakable suffering to Mother Rosa as well. Nothing, however, could now turn her away from what she clearly felt was God’s will.

“And yet, without shedding a tear, I told them. Oh, those two old people, what a scene! They kept an eye on me because they were afraid I would run away. Finally, the moment came; it was morning, the train left at ten, and my friends were waiting for me at the station. Mama, having understood, sat down on the doorstep and said to me:

— I’ll see if you have the courage to pass; you must climb over me!

Papa was crying; in all my life, I had never seen him cry, all the others... it was heartbreaking. I gathered my courage, jumped, climbed over my mother, and stayed outside; I took the stairs in flight and went straight to the station. Thus I began to feel a lion’s courage within me; nothing could impress me anymore.” (Memorie, p. 268).

It was March 13, 1866. In Piacenza, they found that Cogrossi had arranged everything, even forwarding to the Diocesan Authority, on his and Mother Rosa’s behalf, the request for permission for the new Foundation. Mother Rosa and her companions indeed received a warm welcome from the Vicar General, Canons Chiappini, and a few others.

“Most Illustrious Lady, the very reverend Don Luigi Cogrossi has presented to me the pious project of founding in Piacenza a Religious Congregation of women devoted to works of Christian charity; this project is worthy of every encouragement; but my prelate, fully occupied with the labours of his vast diocese, to which he can barely attend, cannot provide any assistance; however, he does not oppose the project, and indeed will rejoice in the good that will be done; the times are sad and unhappy, and seem unfavorable to foundations; yet if the work is willed by the Lord, it will have a happy outcome and correspond to the pious desire of Your Most Illustrious Lady, to whom I offer my respect and veneration” (Canon Prelate Angelo TESTA, Vicar General of the Diocese of Piacenza, 07/02/1866).

Everything, moreover, had to be carried out with great secrecy, since the law suppressing Religious Institutes had already been extended to all regions of Italy subject to Piedmont, and the times were far from favourable to new institutions.

Mother Rosa’s path as a Foundress, from the very beginning, presents itself as difficult and stormy, made up of hopes, optimism, and courageous steps, but also of disappointments, fears, and anguished questions. The strongly adverse political, legal, and economic situation did not discourage her; on the contrary, Mother Rosa showed courage in taking risks: “for those whom He has loved from the beginning, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son”.

Divine Providence is expressed and manifested in the life of Mother Rosa both in the power and in the gentleness that are proper to God. In it, we see confirmed that it is always a mysterious wisdom that encompasses all and fulfils itself in everything, while leaving freedom intact, in the dynamic of personal formation and the development of the world.

Introduction

The meeting in Piacenza with Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a Priest of the Mission and theology professor at the Alberoni College, was of great importance for Mother Rosa. For years, he had nurtured in his heart a desire that had somehow been entrusted to him by the Servant of God, Father Bernardo M. Clausi, of the Minims of Saint Francis of Paola.

Father Bernardo had been very devoted to Saint Anne, whom he venerated as the “grandmother of Jesus”, but especially because he saw in her the Woman chosen by God as an instrument of His providence in the unfolding of the History of Salvation. In her womb, Mary had been conceived, Immaculate from the very first moment of her existence; and the greatness of the privilege of the Daughter also conferred a particular dignity upon the Mother.

Before Mother Rosa, Father Tornatore realised that he had found the instrument he had been waiting for all those years. And to her, who asked him to be her spiritual director, he immediately made the condition that the Institute she was about to found be placed under the title of “Daughters of Saint Anne”.

Mother Rosa, however, who, as she had told the Pope, had always been “entirely devoted to Mary”, had decided to title the Institute “Daughters of the Immaculate Mary, Minims of Saint Francis of Assisi” and was not willing to change. She only decided to do so when a supernatural sign convinced her that Father Tornatore’s proposal was in accordance with God’s will.

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 271)

“As soon as we arrived in this hovel, I looked for a (small) room in better condition to set up a little chapel, which the Bishop blessed and where He left the Lord. Oh, how happy I felt to have my Good with me! And I would spend entire nights there. Oh, what joy I experienced!

One evening, while I was alone and praying deeply, and in the prayer itself felt an intimate union with God, the little chapel was illuminated by a great light. The Most Holy Virgin and Saint Anne appeared to me, and lower down, as if kneeling towards the Most Holy Virgin, Saint Francis of Assisi. The Immaculate, very distinctly, in a clear voice said:

— I desire that the title of the Rules be: “Daughters of Saint Anne,” my mother — and here she pointed to her —. With great satisfaction I entrust this Work to my mother. Do not be distressed; I will always take care of what you do for it.

I remained ecstatic, and as soon as I spoke the last two words, all three disappeared, and it seemed to me that I could still see them, though I said nothing. I stayed this way for a long time, and when I recovered, I realised that much time had passed. What to do? I thought about the obligation to inform the Holy Father if the title had been given, because the ordinances had already been printed with the title of the Immaculate. I could not find peace. I did not want anyone to know this; it was a great torment.”

Only after the first vision of Saint Anne with the Most Holy Mary and Saint Francis of Assisi did Mother Rosa’s relationship with the Holy Mother become deep and intense. Gradually, Saint Anne revealed herself as a special and constant presence in her life and mission.

“…beautiful was the Holy Mother in the act of caressing me: she drew very close and communicated to me a love so strong that, I must confess, I did not know how at all to love her and regard her as a mother” (Memorie, p. 272).

Indeed, after that sign, other clear manifestations followed, and Mother Rosa began to develop an intense love for the Holy Mother of Mary, whereas before, as she confessed, she had no devotion to Saint Anne. In this regard, Father Tornatore played a significant role, seizing every opportunity to transmit and encourage this devotion:

“… Today is the feast of her Heart; I intend to honour it with this image of the great Grandmother of the Blessed Sacrament Jesus, of which one will be placed in each devotional book of her Daughters so that they may be very, very, very devoted. Who knows Saint Anne, the mystery of women! … Saint of Saints! … nothing great worthy of her can be said until it is said that she is the great Mother of the Immaculate.” (Letter of Father Tornatore, May 31, 1866).

In one of the further visions, Saint Anne appeared to her together with Father Bernardo. Mother Rosa knew well that he had loved the Holy Mother greatly during his earthly life and had even prophesied the rise of a Work dedicated to her. Regarding this figure, Mother Rosa describes the experience of his presence alongside Saint Anne:

“While I was in the small chapel of Saint Joseph praying, Saint Anne appeared to me, and on the left side of the Saint was Father Bernardo; both were very beautiful, radiating a vivid light. Saint Anne held a book in her hand and was about to hand it to me. Father Bernardo said to me: ‘Go to Father Tornatore, and tell him to give you the book he holds for this foundation.’ And he disappeared. I remained full of consolation and trust.” (Memorie, p. 139).

Indeed, Fr. Bernardo, who was Fr. Tornatore’s close friend in Rome, had entrusted him with his great desire to found a women’s Congregation dedicated to Saint Anne. And he spoke clearly about it to Fr. Tornatore several times:

“I would be very curious to know whether the Nuns I saw years ago in the month of glorious Saint Anne in a dream (I believe the dream was truly divine) were hers, and who was the one who, with a heavenly air, marked my heart; enough, my Saint Anne to have a family, and the most respectable that has arisen, or is about to arise, in the Church of God!” (Letter of Father Tornatore, July 4, 1866).

From that point onward, Mother Rosa lived her devotion to Saint Anne as a filial relationship and discipleship. Her way of relating to her reflects the Church’s teaching, which forms the faithful in the true veneration of the Saints. The veneration of the Saints does not consist in a multiplicity of outward acts but rather in the intensity of an active love, through which, for the greater good of each person and of the Church itself, one seeks communion with them, participation in their life, and the assistance of their intercession.

From the description Mother Rosa left in her Memoirs of Saint Anne’s presence in her life, the values she developed through living in communion with the Holy Mother of Mary shine through:

“My star Saint Anne marks the day for me every morning, because if I am to experience tribulations, she appears pale and sorrowful; if there are deaths or things that the sisters do that are not right or are against the holy Rule, she is covered with a black veil. If I pray for the health of any benefactor of ours, and they are to die, she immediately makes me aware of it. […] Yes, my Holy Mother, see, it is your honour […] what a beautiful miracle! And to you, my dear Mother, it will redound to your glory and to the light of your Institute!” (Memorie, p. 567).

Because of this divine benevolence, Saint Anne is present in her life and in God’s Work, rejoicing in the good that is accomplished in it, preparing Mother Rosa to face adversities with courage, and sharpening her discernment to distinguish good from evil that offends the Lord and spiritually destroys people. Thus is configured the presence of Saint Anne in her path as a Foundress. The Holy Mother of Mary is, therefore, for her a teacher and maternal guide, a sign of God’s care for Mother Rosa and her Work:

“"...what consolation I experienced when the Holy Mother Anne laughed and, with a gesture of joy, comforted me. Ah! My Mother, are you pleased? Forgive me if I resisted doing your will for fear of making a mistake...” (Memorie, p. 410).

The entire Work, established in the Church by the will of the Father, who, in the Crucified Jesus, addresses the call to Mother Rosa: “From you I want this Work”, is, by His benevolence, placed under the protection of Saint Anne. By carefully rereading Mother Rosa’s experience, we can perceive the deep bond that should unite us as well to the Holy Mother of the Immaculate Mary.

Introduction

Once established in Piacenza, many young women wished to enter the new Institute, and the witness of Mother Rosa and the first Sisters had already crossed the city’s walls.

A little over a year later, Mother Rosa found herself in serious difficulty: in the audience granted to her, Pope Pius IX had urged her to prepare, as soon as possible, a rule suitable for the work and its intended development. The foundress had never stopped thinking about it: “I prayed much”, she wrote, “but I felt nothing”.

Discouraged, Mother Rosa turned to Father Tornatore, who nodded with a smile. Soon the Rule was drafted; it was already February 1868 and had been approved ad experimentum by the Bishop of Piacenza.

Mother Rosa, a devoted daughter of the Church, was not content. Her Work had to be inserted into the heart of the Church because it had been willed and almost imposed by the Holy Father. She therefore sent a copy of the Rule to Rome, so that it might receive the supreme approval of the competent authority.

And here the troubles began. The style and content of the Rule, written by Father Tornatore and surprisingly modern for the time, did not meet the approval of the reviewers.

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 274)

“As soon as they were printed, I took them to Rome, and I was mocked by all the members of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars because they were written in dialogue form: Saint Anne spoke, and then the Daughter responded.

Among them, one jokingly asked if I always spoke with Saint Anne. What embarrassment I suffered together with my secretary, Sister Anna Vincenza! I no longer had the courage to present myself anywhere.

I also brought them to the Holy Father; he said he would read them, always encouraging me. The words of this holy Pope Pius IX meant something to me.

Returning to Piacenza, I will omit what I endured. After a few months, a worthy person wrote to me in complete secrecy, telling me to have the Rules withdrawn from the Bishops who had copies and to burn all those copies I had at home. I immediately carried out these instructions. Then I was told that Mr. Tornatore had been condemned: he could no longer approach the Daughters of Saint Anne, he must no longer come to the house, and no one could even confess to him. In the evening he came, and I communicated this sentence to him. This person also told me to depart immediately for Rome, so I did, and I left at once. Oh, how many sorrows!“

After the first vision, Saint Anne appeared to her again, this time together with Father Bernardo M. Clausi, a Minim of Saint Francis of Paola. He was known to Mother Rosa through the mediation of Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore.

Father Bernardo would become one of God’s messengers for Mother Rosa. He would enlighten her on certain aspects of her mission in the Church and bear witness through his presence to her identification with elements of the Mystery of Christ, the Trinity, Mary Most Holy, and the Immaculate Maternity of Saint Anne. Moreover, he was the one who, in the name of God, would indicate to Mother Rosa the person who should collaborate with her in drafting the Rule to be written:

“One evening, while I was alone in the chapel, behold, Saint Anne and Father Bernardo appeared to me […] Father Bernardo said these words:

— The regulation that you desire, tell him to have Mr. Tornatore do it.” (Memorie, p. 272)

Mother Rosa did not have the courage to tell Father Tornatore what Father Bernardo had instructed her, and she waited several months. In her Memoirs, she describes how Father Bernardo appeared to her several times, insisting that she carry out this step “out of obedience”.

“— Go at once and tell him that it is I who send you; that he should make this regulation immediately. How much distress I felt! But I resolved to go, and so I did. I went to this Mr. Tornatore and, halfway, told him what Father Bernardo had said to me.

He began to laugh and replied:

— I will do it. And so he did.” (Memorie, p. 274).

Here we see that God, in His salvific economy, has created and continues to create men and women with different roles so that they may collaborate with Him, in Christ and in the Holy Spirit, in the building of His Kingdom. He accompanies the development of the Work entrusted to Mother Rosa through the assistance of people specially prepared by Him:

“My daughter Benedetta in Jesus, […] The venerable Father Bernardo M. Clausi is the one whom the Lord used to found the Institute. You may ask me: how? If I have not told you before, I tell you now […] The Lord, in order to make known to the Mother that this was His will, caused Mother Saint Anne and His faithful servant, the venerable Father Bernardo, to appear to the Mother and make her understand that it was pleasing to God that the Institute be the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. And in this vision, the Venerable held in his hand the book of the Rules and told the Mother that I held this book and that it should be obtained from me […] And so, I then wrote the Rules...” (Father Tornatore to a Daughter of Saint Anne).

Indeed, Father Tornatore would write the Rule. But, as mentioned previously, the style and content of the Rule he drafted did not meet the approval of the reviewers in Rome:

“These Rules, due to the slanders of my enemies, were burned by order of the Holy Office. The Mother said: the Rules burned, made by the Father, will come out of the fire; and this was a prophecy; because, despite many attempts to make new Rules, no one ever succeeded. Ah, and again, by the will of our Cardinal Protector, Cardinal Berardi, I had to make them myself; and these are the common Rules that are now in use.” (Ibidem).

After a long and anxious wait, on February 19, 1872, Mother Rosa received the order to destroy all copies of the Rule and to remove its author. This was a very painful blow: Father Tornatore was now considered a true father to the Daughters of Saint Anne, and the Rule he had written had been received as the authentic code of life capable of leading the Sisters to holiness.

It is true that this was not an easy spirituality, but the Father, as master and guide, explaining and commenting on its meaning, went far beyond the rigid juridical conception that would have informed Religious Life of the time. The time was not yet mature. It would take the Second Vatican Council for the Rule, resurfaced from the oblivion of a century, to find its full and legitimate place in the spirit of renewed Religious Life.

Father Tornatore suffered the blow and withdrew into a dignified and painful silence. Yet he had to leave the Daughters of Saint Anne, whom he now loved more than himself. He would patiently await a second “hour of God”, which would come in 1876, when the Cardinal Protector of the Institute, urged and implored by Mother Rosa, worked to obtain their reinstatement.

The story of the Rule would conclude later. After further unsuccessful attempts by Mother Rosa and several other ecclesiastics appointed by the Holy See, Father Tornatore would rewrite it in a more juridical and less spiritual style than the first. After several adjustments and an experimental period of seven years, it would receive definitive approval in 1892, as a gift from the Holy See to Mother Rosa for the 25th anniversary of her religious profession.

It cannot be said that the Rule of 1869, once destroyed, ceased to exist; it remained alive in the consciousness of Mother Rosa and the Daughters of Saint Anne. She had received and recognised it as a true expression of God’s will for the newly begun Work. The Mother continued to live it faithfully until her death, offering in herself the clearest and most certain key to its interpretation and application, as an example and teaching for the entire Family of Saint Anne.

Introduction

The new Institute was born under the banner of absolute poverty, yet guided by a surge of charity that never refused any request from the sick and the poor. The Sisters visited and cared for them at home and also, always free of charge, in hospitals both day and night. To live and provide necessities for those they assisted, they also begged for alms.

The people of Piacenza first observed these young women with a critical eye, but soon with admiration, seeing how lovingly available and always serious they were — distinguished even in performing the humblest services. Instinctively, they nicknamed them: “the Genoese women”.

The Work had been established for less than a year when a terrible cholera epidemic broke out in Italy, reaching Piacenza and its surroundings, causing hundreds of deaths in just two months. Mother Rosa and the Daughters of Saint Anne were ready to devote themselves to caring for the afflicted, fearless of the risk of contagion, from which they all remained immune, attributing it to a special protection of Saint Anne.

“These [Sisters] must devote themselves to the growth of our holy Faith and to the care of the sick at home, and they will also receive sick Daughters to teach them Christian doctrine and women’s work. To the sick people they assist, if they are poor, they will bring whatever is necessary, and all will be free of charge.” (From the Rules).

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Circular Letter, 1876)

“The Lord has raised up our Institute so that it might be the family of the glorious Saint Anne, August Mother of the Immaculate; in this family, the great Saint would be honoured, loved, and imitated. In general, the Sisters respond to this purpose. They imitate the life that their Mother led on this earth for the good of her neighbour.

The service they provide to the sick, both in hospitals and at home, is carried out in a spirit of faith and with love and sacrifice, which clearly shows that they keep in mind the divine words of Jesus Christ, who assures that the care done for the sick for His love is considered done to Himself…

What gratitude does God ask of us for the favours with which He has filled us in the year now ended? He desires a profound sense of humility, by which we acknowledge that we have not deserved them. Humility that makes us offer Him all the praise that the Institute receives from His creatures and makes us confess before His Divine Majesty that we are unworthy servants, unable even to accomplish what we are obliged to do.”

Purified by suffering and humiliation, Mother Rosa discovered, so to speak, her own identity in her dedication to the sick and the poor, assisting them both in hospitals and at home.

“In the year 1857, freed from all obligations, I devoted myself with greater fervour to works of piety and to visiting hospitals, assisting the poor sick at home, helping them as much as I could and serving them in every way.” (Memorie, p. 93)

There was an instinct in her — imperious and strong — that drove her by vocation towards the poor and sick, towards young women at risk of sin and losing their dignity as daughters of God, towards every man and woman in need: in them she always found the image of her Crucified Lord, who now filled her heart.

“I went to the hospital, where I found all my happiness, because nothing discouraged me and nothing disgusted me. Cleaning the wounds was the thing I most enjoyed, because it seemed to me that I was doing it for my dear Jesus.” (Memorie, p. 123)

Having become a foundress, she wished, through the zeal of the Daughters of Saint Anne, to meet every bodily and spiritual need, every social wound. She therefore sought to instill in them the original character of the Institute and the charity that moved her to self-giving, in the style shaped by the Holy Mother of the Immaculate Mary.

“Ah! You always converse with Jesus, because in touching those sick with charity—and that charity so great that your dear Mother Saint Anne had—oh, tell them so that you may also share it, for in those sick creatures Jesus is found. Ah! What a thought, my daughters!” (Letters, vol. I, 11.6)

She communicated to her Daughters, both in person and through letters, the fruitful richness of her spiritual and apostolic experience. She guided them in daily circumstances, which were not always easy or favourable, so that they could live the gift coherently, helping them translate her charismatic insights into concrete acts of charity.

“I assure you that I feel as if dying from the desire to come, to be with you, to take part in your charity. Yes, soon, I hope, and it is this alone that makes me work night and day, so I can fly close to those I love so much, namely the sick and you, my dear little daughters.” (Letters, vol. I, 11.7)

Her preference was for the poor and the sick, but her charity extended to all. In the various foundations, the initial work of charity was almost always home care for the sick; even in those whose purpose was schooling, free assistance to the sick could not be lacking.

“The moral education of young girls of the people and free home assistance to the sick are the primary purpose of the Institute itself.” (Letters, vol. II, 23.2)

The cholera epidemic of 1867 was like a trial by fire for the nascent Institute, and the more general epidemic of 1884 – 1887 served almost as a public test: the Daughters of Saint Anne gave themselves heroically, especially in Naples and Sicily; some died victims of the contagion.

“An Institute is in the prime of observance when the Spirit of Jesus Christ reigns in it. The Spirit of Jesus Christ manifests itself primarily in the charity that drove Him to die for us. Now, of this Spirit, by the mercy of God, the Institute was full even in this year.

The Lord afflicted the poor city of Palermo with cholera. While people, terrified by this terrible pestilence, fled here and there, and the poor struck by the disease were left abandoned, our sisters, full of the charity of Jesus Christ, went into the midst of the havoc; and day and night they brought every kind of comfort, and did not abandon the victims except when they were healed, or when they had entrusted their spirit to God and their body to the tomb. This spirit of evangelical courage, which cheerfully faced the dangers of death to save the life of their brothers, astonished not only the good but also the enemies of our holy religion; and in this way, Jesus Christ, source of so much charity, was glorified by both the good and the afflicted.” (Circular Letter, 1886).

The legitimate pride of the Foundress for the heroism of her Daughters is reflected in the circular letters of these years. She called the Daughters of Saint Anne the “poor servants of the poor” (Letter to Princess Emilia of Italy, 12 May 1893).

After the epidemic ended, Mother Rosa welcomed dozens of orphaned girls into their Mother House and founded the first orphanage. She did not limit herself to providing material and moral assistance to the orphans; even with very limited resources, she provided them with education and professional training. No form of human misery — material, moral, or spiritual — left her unmoved: she cared for the sick, orphaned children, the elderly… for the poor in general.

Soon, numerous requests arrived from bishops and administrators of pious works, asking that a community of Daughters of Saint Anne be established in their institutions, since they had always distinguished themselves by heroic charity. Whenever possible, Mother Rosa consented, even sending postulants and novices.

Introduction

The first sisters close to Mother Rosa reflected the community that had formed around a truly fruitful Charism. This shows, therefore, a progressive growth in Grace, in fraternal communion, in Christian charity, and in the divine inspiration that called them to be the “Daughters of Saint Anne”, and which soon saw them “grow in the affection of the peoples” (cf. Circular of 1880).

For this reason, the Congregation quickly moved towards openness “to the Peoples”: with the dispatch of the first 16 Sisters “to the New World” (cf. Circular of 1879). The Congregation saw its expansion across the seas, first to America and then to Africa, and gradually to all five continents, with a sensitivity of its own, shaped by the thought, way of being, and lifestyle of Mother Rosa Gattorno and her many Daughters.

By the grace of God and abundant blessings, the Daughters of Saint Anne were able to extend their presence to various parts of the world, signifying not only the vitality of the Charism, but also calling attention to the missionary and universal character of the Congregation: “This zeal of our Sisters arises from seeing the prosperous results that the peoples who receive them reap, both in the Hospitals and in the Schools…” (cf. Circular of 1880).

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 261)

“Oh, I will never forget this day! My hopes vanished and a most bitter knife came to wound me deeply […]

I had already had the Rules given to the Supreme Pontiff—those which my dear Crucified Lord had dictated to me and which, according to the words of the Holy Father, were like the commandments. As soon as I was at his holy feet, Pius IX blessed me, and when I rose, holding my hand firmly in his, he told me that he had read those Rules, that they were truly beautiful, and that I should not delay in putting them into practice […]

— No, Your Holiness — I replied — I wish to do the will of God.

He answered:

— Good.

Then, as if inspired, he said to me:

— This Institute will spread rapidly like the flight of a dove to all parts of the world; God will take care of your children, you think of God in His work.

What a prophecy! Dear Holy Father! I rose and could scarcely utter a word; I felt as though my chest would burst. He led me to his desk and gave me two of his photographs, writing a motto on each one. Oh, how I felt!“

The Institute expanded with astonishing speed in both numbers and works. And not only in Italy: by 1878, just twelve years after its foundation, sixteen Daughters of St. Anne left Italy to establish, after a long and adventurous journey, two houses in La Paz, Bolivia. This marked the beginning of the fulfillment of Pope Pius IX’s prophetic words: “This Institute will spread rapidly like the flight of a dove to all parts of the world”.

The Sisters, faithful to Mother Rosa’s inspiration, truly made themselves available to carry out a charismatic and universal mission, collaborating within the Church and with the Church in the Salvific Work, in a maternal spirit of dedication. They were always committed to presenting, to all peoples and especially to the poorest, the merciful face of the Father.

“What the Holy Father told me the first time I was at his feet is being fulfilled: there will be so many apostles that they will spread throughout the world. Oh! Great Holy Father Pius IX!” (Letter to Cardinal Patrizi, 23/12/1874).

With this vision, Mother Rosa took the opportunity to send the first missionary Sisters and encouraged them, with a prophetic spirit, to cross the nation’s borders to testify to God’s saving will in the universal mission of the Church. She understood the need for the missionary renewal that the Church was experiencing, to regain vigour in responding to Jesus’ perpetual invitation: “Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations”.

The prompt willingness of the Sisters, besides being a response to this “further insight” of Mother Rosa, answered the many needs in different parts of the Church, so that Jesus, her Supreme Good, could be known and loved everywhere. Testimony to this zeal can be found in the beautiful words of the Bolivian press welcoming the first missionary Sisters:

“Sisters of Charity, angels who soften the miseries of life, the tribulations of beggars, and the pains of human existence with goodness and consolation; messengers of peace amid the torments of hunger and misery that afflict Bolivia: welcome! ... Archangels of mercy and charity! ... Women of Charity! Blessed be the hour of your arrival in this Republic! Your mission is holy, and blessed be your Institution, for it spreads consolation and charity ... just as God gave manna in the desert.” (from the newspaper “La Tribuna”, 24 January 1879)

The Daughters of St. Anne have always been, in many places, “pioneering religious women”, especially in the fields of Health and Education. They also inaugurated a new era for the apostolic female Consecrated Life, making a significant contribution to the Church and society.

“The Heavenly Father, who planted in the garden of His Church, looks upon our Institute with special favour [...] The service the Sisters render to the sick is carried out in the spirit of faith and with loving sacrifice, which clearly shows that they keep in mind the divine words of Jesus Christ, who assures us that the care given to the sick for His love is counted as done to Himself [...] no less vigilant is the care of those employed in teaching: to imitate the piety of our Holy Mother […]” (Circular Letter, 1876).

For us today, this style of Mother Rosa and the first Sisters is a model of active participation in the life of the universal Church, made present both in the local and missionary Church; with the awareness that it is in the daily fabric that true dedication to the entire Church is lived.

“[...] So courage, the Holy Pope Pius IX told me, we will be like many apostles; our Institute will spread to all parts of the world. So how can I fear with this before my eyes? I pray that God sends us a little providence, but for nothing else [...] We sail with full sails without me doing anything. Yes, I will always say it, and I can confirm that I have done nothing for this Work. The Lord has done everything […]” (Letter to the Sisters of Sampierdarena, 25/02/1871).

The Daughters of St. Anne and all members of the entire Charismatic Family, in communion with the Church, strive to respond to all current challenges as a prophetic voice: working for the integral formation of new generations, families, and educators; caring for the sick and the poor; and promoting the growth of the Holy Faith, bearing fruits of humanity and solidarity for society and the Church.

“Courage, my daughter, show yourself a generous daughter of our Mother St. Anne, a daughter detached from all, a daughter who seeks nothing but the interest, delight, and glory of her great Holy Mother, who cannot accept anything less than generous hearts, which for her love are ready to go, to be anywhere, to set out for Jesus and for all things in her Work […]” (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, 1867).

Following in the footsteps of Mother Rosa and the first Daughters of Saint Anne, we too want to rediscover our role in pastoral ministry, under the banner of communion, participation and mission.

After more than a century and a half, the small seed has grown. The Daughters of St. Anne continue to serve Christ in their brothers and sisters with the maternal and merciful heart of God. And with them, all of us draw from the ever - relevant and dynamic source of our Charism and Spirituality to live our mission, which today is particularly challenging due to the process of changing times, amid difficult social and political contexts, often opposed to the Church and its Works.
