Introduction

With a sense of humble gratitude, we truly believe that the Family of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, was born not from a merely human plan, but by the initiative of God. It is a small part of the People of God which, moved by the Holy Spirit to respond to a free call from the Father, has gathered to work “in the Lord’s field”, collaborating in the Church and with the Church in the saving work of Christ (cf. Circular Letter, 1876).

For this reason, we recognise that the entire Charismatic Family is rooted in the inspiration of Blessed Mother Rosa Gattorno (cf. Memorie, p. 624), in whose heart vibrated the intuition regarding the various foundations, which would share a single spirit (Charism) and would all fully participate in all the spiritual merits of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Animated by this urgent inner impulse, Mother Rosa repeatedly writes in her Memorie: “Remember the three drops of my blood that I showed you and shed on your heart; I told you that they would be the three Orders that you must [found]” (cf. Memorie, p. 665).

And coming to the year 1991, with the 18th General Chapter of the Daughters of Saint Anne, the long-awaited hour seems finally to have arrived for Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno. The Institute, docile to the “breath of the Spirit”, embraces the “New Life”, recognising its charism-inspired imprint.

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memorie, p. 261)

“A poor soul, so alone, with an abyss of matters to attend to, and also this which for me is the most dreadful thing that could exist: even the mere thought that I might do the slightest thing that is not His will…

Oh, how painful this is! I do not know how to describe it! To decide to let it go? Oh, how could I do that? What if I were mistaken?

And then I hear repeated within me:

— Remember the three drops of my blood that I showed you and that I poured upon your heart; I told you that they would be the three Orders that you must [found].

— Oh my Love, how can this be — I say within myself — I who am so old, how will I manage? I am full of sufferings, ill, and I feel that I can no longer go on. It is true that You make the dead live and the dying work, for I can say that my suffering is a daily agony; I do not speak of the pains, because it would take too long.”

With the invitation of the Second Vatican Council to “return to the sources”, the Sisters, Daughters of Saint Anne, having obtained permission from the Church to reopen the archives containing the writings of Mother Rosa — sealed due to her beatification process in Piacenza and Rome — found themselves faced with numerous documents in which they discovered an immense charismatic, spiritual, and historical richness. Meanwhile, the Spirit Himself was raising up, from North to South, from East to West, those whom He desired to be formed by this Charism.

From 1984, the Superior General at the time, Sr. A. Virginia Sinagra, listening to the desire of these individuals to share in the Institute’s spirituality—while living their own particular states of life and leaving space for the action of the Spirit - became increasingly attentive to any manifestation of this new vitality of the Charism, considering it a special initiative of God in the history of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Considering also the numerical consistency of the requests, the validity of the proofs provided by the aspirants themselves and attested by the Sisters who had accompanied the emergence and development of spontaneous groups, as well as the positive judgment of the Provincial Superiors and the letters of numerous Bishops, the Mother deemed it appropriate to inform the Sisters gathered in Chapter about the reality of these developments.

“For about nine years, alongside various Communities of the Daughters of Saint Anne scattered throughout the world, groups of laypeople and priests have arisen, eager to share in the spirituality of the Institute […]. There are even about ten priests and young aspirants to the priesthood who would like to shape their priestly lives according to our spirituality. This emerging richness and variety of life, one might say spontaneous, alongside our communities in the various continents, was carefully considered during the Chapter and the subject of humble prayer.” (NEW LIFE, Acts of the 18th General Chapter, 1991. Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne).

Therefore, during the 18th General Chapter of the Daughters of Saint Anne, held in Rome from December 3 to January 28, 1991, the Chapter members approved the request, repeatedly presented by several aspirants, to be aggregated in various canonical forms to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

This “New Life”, nurtured within the Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne, reveals to the Church and to History the richness and fruitfulness of the gift God granted to Blessed Mother Anna Rosa Gattorno.

“In [distant] vision I saw many great things for our Institute; a light allowed me to see the great panorama of the Order in the future. I must say that the divine [project] was so beautiful and intricate that I was ecstatic and delighted while I saw in it a river of numerous sufferings...” (Memorie, p. 320)

Despite her zealous concern, the projects undertaken in her time took other forms, for which the Mother herself repeatedly wondered whether they were in accordance with the will of God. In her Memorie, she writes, with regret, on the matter:

“The work of the tertiaries, and moreover arranged with the Bishop? This will not be it, but rather some other [thing] for which one will have to struggle...” (Memorie, p. 664)

“The uninitiated work of the Sons of Saint Anne gives me great sorrow, because I see that it is not as God desires it… […] I see and feel that Jesus does not find His delight...” (Memorie, p. 853)

Sustained by the certainty that, at the proper time, God’s hour would arrive, Mother Rosa entrusted the realisation of these singular plans to Divine Providence. The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne would, at various other moments in history, seek to give life to her inspirations, seeking other juridical forms more in harmony with the times. But, as with every plan of God, His hour must be awaited.

For this reason, we believe that in 1991, for the entire Family of Saint Anne, the long-awaited hour of God finally seemed to have arrived for Mother Rosa. It is the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne itself, docile to God’s will and attentive to the signs of the times, which, after hearing from various authoritative persons, gave form and continuity to the different inspirations that the Mother had received from her Beloved Crucified:

“The Chapter members unanimously felt inspired to accept their repeatedly expressed request to be aggregated or associated in a precise canonical form with the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. Therefore, it was unanimously decided to add to the 3rd article of the Constitutions the following statement: ‘By virtue of this spirit, the Family of the Daughters of Saint Anne is open to receiving other forms of evangelical life that are inspired by the same charism’.” (NEW LIFE, Acts of the 18th General Chapter, 1991. Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne).

In this regard, the Chapter approved inserting a new chapter into the Constitutions, with the following formulation:

“AGGREGATIONS AND ASSOCIATIONS. Open to the universal breath of the Spirit, which incessantly raises up new forms of life wherever, whenever, and however He wills, the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne is ready to welcome those forms of evangelical life in which it recognises the imprint of its Charism and which, as such, are confirmed by the authority of the Church. And, constantly striving towards the greater good of brothers and the extension of the Kingdom, it gives thanks to the Father for every gift.” (Constitutions of the Sisters, Daughters of Saint Anne, art. 191).

This is the living and concrete testimony that the Daughters of Saint Anne, “open to the universal breath of the Spirit”, hand down to the entire Charismatic Family, which, in this new time, consolidates Mother Rosa’s “dream”, confident that their docility will help God’s will continue to be fulfilled in and through them.

“Around every Religious Family, as well as around Societies of Apostolic Life and Secular Institutes, there exists a larger family, the ‘Charismatic Family,’ which includes several Institutes that recognise the same Charism, and above all lay Christians who feel called, each in their own condition, to share in the same charismatic reality.” (Pope Francis, on the occasion of the Year of Consecrated Life, III-1).

In light of what Pope Francis has written, we too are growing in awareness that no Charism is self-sufficient. Every Charism, entrusted to the hands of a founder or foundress, is destined for the entire People of God and, only if welcomed and lived by the various members of the People of God, can it fully unleash its potential.

Along this path, for over 40 years, the Charismatic Family of Saint Anne, founded by Blessed Anna Rosa Gattorno, can be considered a fruitful reality within the Church: the Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, the Contemplative Perpetual Adorers Daughters of Saint Anne, the Religious Institute of the Sons of Saint Anne, the Secular Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, and the Movement of Hope.

“In faithful response to a common charismatic call, and conscious of being members of the same family, forge bonds of friendship in fraternal charity and nurture the hope of reaching the same ideal.”

(Cfr. Documents of base, p. 11).

The Charismatic Family of Saint Anne is made up of different Institutes and a Movement — people of various states of life: laypeople, religious sisters and brothers, priests, and secular members — who recognise themselves as belonging to the same Charism of Mother Rosa. Through her, we are united with one another in the fraternity of Christ, a supernatural climate realised in our common identification with Him and, in Him, with our brothers and sisters, and manifested in a communion of prayer and life (cfr. Documents of base, p. 12).

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memoirs, p. 133)

“I was in church with my eyes fixed on the tabernacle, praying that he would take away certain thoughts about a conversation I had had, but they kept growing; this person was afraid of persecution and I had seen that she was agitated as she spoke to me about it. Then a voice said to me: «You will tell — and here he told me the name of this person — that she will never have a part in the great tribulations: first [of all] because she does not have the strength to bear them. God [has] accepted your sacrifice and everything will be laid upon your head: you alone, alone, will have to bear it all».

And afterwards that voice showed me many things; they were dreadful things that were soon to happen to me. But so great was the strength he gave me that at so horrible a sight I felt no fear, and never did I fail in a single thought for the Work of my Lord. Yes, let your victim be consumed, but may she never fail in your loving service.

Oh, my dear Love, the painful and heart-rending sufferings you announced to me were not slow in coming. I am deprived of everything within, I am in agony, I feel I have a strength that is not mine but my Good's, because without it I would collapse.”

The inspiration Mother Rosa received for a Branch of Contemplative Life in her Work gradually became clearer to her in intimacy with the Lord, through the supernatural experiences He granted her and through events that urged her to act accordingly.

In her autobiographical accounts, in her Memoirs, Mother Rosa tells of a further vision granted to her by Fr Bernardo M. Clausi of “another new foundation of cloistered nuns”. So, when she writes of the vision of the “three drops”, she considered that this might be one of the “three Orders” she was to found: “I thought it was to be the branch of Daughters of Saint Anne of contemplative, cloistered life!” (Memoirs, p. 624). And very probably she thought so too when, in 1884, the community of the “Tertiaries of Saint Anne, Perpetual Adorers of the Most Blessed Sacrament” began.

Historical circumstances had set before her this project conceived by the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Giovanni Battista Scalabrini, whose main purpose would be adoration of the Blessed Sacrament, the making and care of sacred vestments and the care of deaf-mute girls. Accepting the proposal, she carried it forward with a mother's spirit and a great sense of responsibility. Yet, in relation to her first intuition about the Contemplative Life, it seemed very clear to her that this project, at least in this form, did not correspond to it:

“I fear that it is not God's will that I take charge of the ’Third Order of Saint Anne’. […] The Work of the tertiaries, and moreover set up together with the Bishop? It will not be this, but rather some other [thing] for which we will have to fight. Oh, already I am fighting the enemy, who wages a war within me more horrible than ever. It arouses in me such restlessness and aversion that I do not know how to overcome it. It keeps urging me to leave it and not put my hand to it…“ (Memoirs, p. 664)

But just as God's works are born and develop according to the times and rhythms He himself sets, so it was for Mother Rosa. Preserved in the historical Archive of the Religious Institute, however, is a copy of the Constitutions of the “Daughters of Saint Anne Perpetual Adorers”, outlining a structure of Contemplative Life different from that of the “Tertiaries of Saint Anne”.

There remains, however, uncertainty about the person who was to have founded the “Daughters of Saint Anne Perpetual Adorers”. Here is one testimony:

“Sr A. Maria Teresa Sorrentino, when she was still in the world, was herself thinking of becoming the foundress of an Institute, at the suggestion of Cardinal Guarino. Mother Rosa liked this young woman very much and wanted her in her Institute, and one day she said to me about Maria Teresa's plan to found: ‘to found an Institute you need a chest of bronze’.” (Princess Emilia di Fitalia, AFSA C.1.139/12)

There is also an undated autograph of Mother Rosa with some corrections to a Rule of Life and some points dictated to the Princess di Fitalia. In the first document the Mother expresses, with her usual determination, her clear will that the new foundation be bound in every respect to the original Institute and that there be no distinction of any kind within the Community. Some particularly incisive expressions are given here:

“[…] I cannot allow the three Sisters to withdraw once the Institute is running on its own, not that […]; nor can I allow [a] separate house standing on its own […] The title of Eucharistic Heart may be given to the House, but not to the Sisters, nor may they have a distinctive sign, not that; we must be perfectly equal […]” (AFSA C.I.135/5)

What the concrete reasons were for which the Work then remained only a plan and could not be carried out, we are not given to know. We do know, however, that Sorrentino entered the Institute on 8 March 1892, received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 17 April of the same year and was given the name Sr A. Maria Teresa. She worked closely with Mother Rosa in delicate offices, even as Assistant General, while continuing to be Superior of the Community of Via d’Ossuna – Palermo.

But since God leaves no chapter unfinished, a century after Mother Rosa's inspiration three Sisters of the Daughters of Saint Anne felt God's call to live a style of life more devoted to prayer and to adoration of Jesus in the Eucharist. Some of them received “inner words” and others “particular signs” from the Spirit, in perfect correspondence with what had once been inspired in Mother Rosa. Here are some of these expressions:

“On 20 September 1989 these words resounded in my soul: ‘Contemplatives without bars for the mission of the Institute’. Others followed on 29 September: ‘Hand the gift over to the Mother’; on other occasions, deep within, these too: ‘Adorers’; ‘Stand beneath the Cross with Mary and Mother Rosa’; on 10 August 1987: ‘Whom shall I send? – Send me’; ‘Sacrifice-holocaust-adore’; on 11 August: ‘Uselessness-adoration’; ’Contemplative Daughters of St Anne’.” (Mother Virginia Sinagra, Virga Jesse X, no. 3 of 1994, p. 8).

They kept and pondered in their hearts what the Spirit was suggesting, until the supreme authority of the Institute pronounced on the matter. From 1986 onwards He continued to inspire the persons who were to begin the foundation, and the essential elements that define its character in the Family of Saint Anne and in the Church.

The 18th General Chapter of the Daughters of Saint Anne also marked for them the acceptance of the “gift” and the start of the Work. As early as 1992 the first three Sisters (two Brazilian and one Italian) were summoned to Rome to discern together with the Mother General and her Council.

During the year 1992-1993, in Erice (TP), Italy (a place the Lord had shown in a moment of prayer in 1986), the Sisters drafted the parts of the Constitutions for the Contemplative Branch, testing them in daily life.

In 1993, when the lines for embodying the “gift” received from the Lord had already been traced, Sr A. Graça Guimarães returned to Brazil to open the second Community, where the Bishop emeritus had already prepared the building. Sr A. Rosaria De Simone, meanwhile, remained in Erice to carry on the Work begun, together with other Sisters who gradually felt drawn to this discernment.

As for the canonical structure, the following General Chapter (1996/1997) examined and approved its nature in accordance with the Sisters' inspirations, which corresponded to Mother Rosa's own. They conceived it as a charismatic part of the whole Family of Saint Anne. And just as Mother Rosa had expressed in her intention, the Sisters, even before knowing her thought, had perceived it as a value:

“In the great tree of the Charismatic Family […] they are placed at the root, in the place of silence and anonymity, from which flows their specific function of being, through adoration, prayer and offering, a supplicating strength for all humanity, for the Church and for the Charismatic Family engaged in missionary apostolic service.” (Constitutions of the Contemplative FSA, art. 5.1).

This, unlike the other expressions in the Family of Saint Anne, allows us to see them not as a “detached arm” but as a “Branch intrinsically united to it”:

“The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne recognises the ‘Daughters of Saint Anne Contemplative Perpetual Adorers’ as a ‘Branch’ intrinsically united to itself (Constitutions of the FSA, art. 198 c).

And this further project, too, springing from Mother Rosa's heart, can today be called a happy reality, now that Daughters of Saint Anne, drawn to this other particular way of living the Charism, have felt called to take on with their religious consecration the dimension of Contemplatives and Perpetual Adorers:

“Institutes completely devoted to contemplation, composed of either women or men, are for the Church a reason for pride and a source of heavenly graces. By their lives and mission, the members of these Institutes imitate Christ in his prayer on the mountain, bear witness to God's lordship over history and anticipate the glory which is to come. In solitude and silence, by listening to the word of God, participating in divine worship, personal asceticism, prayer, mortification and the communion of fraternal love, they direct the whole of their lives and all their activities to the contemplation of God. In this way they offer the ecclesial community a singular testimony of the Church's love for her Lord, and they contribute, with hidden apostolic fruitfulness, to the growth of the People of God. Thus there is good reason to hope that the different forms of contemplative life will experience growth in the younger Churches as an expression of the complete rooting of the Gospel, especially in those areas of the world where other religions prevail. This will make it possible to bear witness to the vitality of the traditions of Christian asceticism and mysticism and will contribute to interreligious dialogue.” (Vita Consecrata, 8).

After reading no. 8 of the Apostolic Exhortation Vita Consecrata, reflection can be deepened with the following questions:

  1. How open are we to the “gift” of the Spirit? Are we able to read his promptings in our daily lives?

  2. The Contemplative Daughters of St Anne offer themselves, with Mother Rosa and like her, as victims of expiation. And we, how do we share in this offering?

  3. And we, how do we live the centrality of the Eucharist in our daily lives, according to our specific vocation?

Introduction

It seems truly fitting to us that, in this year in which the Holy Father has chosen to devote his General Audience catecheses to the documents of the Second Vatican Council, we should reflect more deeply on the “New Life” and, in particular, on the vocation of the members of the Movement of Hope.

These Brothers and Sisters are called to live in the world as a Sign of Hope, starting from their own condition as lay people and from our common Charism: “You lay people too can live the spirituality of the Daughters of Saint Anne, be their ‘hundred arms’ and reach where they cannot reach” (Rita Di Maggio, 09/12/1981).

In this regard we can affirm today with greater conviction: the lay person in the Church and in the Family of Saint Anne is, and always will be, a Christian who “sanctifies the world from within”.

For this reason it is very important to understand that their call to be a Sign of Hope becomes their “way of life”, their way of being present in society, in line with the vocation of the whole Family of Saint Anne; and also the path to follow for evangelisation and missionary action in communion with the local Church, in a society where faith can no longer be taken for granted. For the members of the Movement of Hope this becomes a vocation within the Vocation.

“Oh, my Love, I am ready! Alas, what have I done? How beautiful he was! He stood still a moment, came towards me with open arms and vanished. Oh, my Love, yes, I am coming to receive you! And I hurried to the church to receive him. Oh, what I felt! Tell it, my Good, you alone could tell it! Oh, you who are my Paradise, what can I do to make you known to the whole world! The ‘Movement of Hope’, so called from 24 May 1989, is rooted in the inspiration of Mother Rosa Gattorno. In confirmation of this we can refer to the testimony of Princess Emilia Settimo di Fitalia, Mother Rosa's spiritual daughter, in her Deposition for the Roman Process of her Cause of Canonisation (Session 319, p. 2451v.):

“When Mother Gattorno was about to come to Palermo, Sr Anna del Salvatore spoke to me about her with great enthusiasm, wishing me to know her too. On her arrival she herself introduced me to the servant of God [...] Our conversation (which was also the only one during that first visit of hers to Sicily) turned on a plan of hers to found a Third Order of Daughters of Saint Anne; a plan that would also have extended to men. She promised me, of her own accord, that she would enrol me too in this Third Order, and that in this way I too would share in all the merits of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. I believe I belong to this Third Order, as do my husband, Cardinal di Belmonte and Monsignor Briuccia...” (Positio super virtutibus, p. 427).

This further “inspiration” of Mother Rosa was taken up by the Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which tried several times to organise it in various juridical forms, without success. In fact, 24 years after her death, it reappeared as a lay association, ‘Friends of the Daughters of Saint Anne’. And it made its way forward again, being given careful consideration during their Special Chapter of 1969-1971 and in the subsequent General Chapters of 1972 and 1978.

This “Project” regained vigour and then took ever clearer shape, becoming a Movement, through the intuition of Rita Di Maggio, who, during the solemn celebration of 9 December 1981 for the transfer of Mother Rosa's venerated mortal remains from the General House to the Church of Saint Anne at the Lateran, felt the urge to spread Mother Rosa's Charism among the laity:

“You lay people too can live the spirituality of the Daughters of Saint Anne, be their ‘hundred arms’ and reach where they cannot reach.” (Rita Di Maggio, 09/12/1981)

The Lord calls not on the basis of our merits or abilities but according to his plan. He himself prepares, forms and places alongside us the people who are to collaborate in carrying it out.

By a providential gift Rita had the grace of living through the events of the Special Chapter, so called because the Second Vatican Council had invited all Institutes to “return to the sources”. Indeed, the Basic Documents are the fruit of that event, and Rita had the grace of tasting that richness of the Charism right from its sources, with Sisters who had taken part in the Special Chapter and worked on drafting the Documents.

She thus understood that this particular call was not to live as “Friends of the Daughters of Saint Anne” or “of Mother Rosa”, but to live their own particular Charism:

“It was not a matter of living like a group of ladies of charity, nor of contemplating in Mother Rosa the ‘woman already a saint’. It was a matter of living her Charism and her spirituality as lay people.” (Rita Di Maggio, 2001).

She thought that, to act as a “bridge”, it was important to invite people who had had experience with the Daughters of St Anne, but none of them ever joined except Maria Raimondi, who was not on that list but whom the Lord allowed in by ways known only to him. The first meeting was held at her home in Foggia on 16 May 1982. That date also marks the presence of Fr Sergio Angelini, who, when invited, replied that “if it was God's Work, he would be available”. And he served this Work of God until his last breath, on 28 April 2025.

Until early 1985 they enjoyed no official recognition from the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. But in that year the then Superior General, Mother A. Virginia Sinagra, with the consent of her Council, asked them to live the experience with a more attentive openness to the signs of the Spirit. The need was felt to set up the Central Team, made up of Rita Di Maggio, Maria Raimondi, Arcangelo Aurino with his wife Sofia, Carmela De Maio, the General Councillor Sr A. Angela Florio and Fr Sergio Angelini as priest and guide.

In December 1985 they drew up the first plan for their group, shared by the Mother General and her Council; this marked a decisive moment for setting out confidently on their journey, with the support, above all charismatic, of the Institute.

At the same time Mother Virginia took care to present their reality to the Church, writing to the Bishops in whose Dioceses groups had sprung up, and in particular, in December 1987, she submitted their first rule to the Congregation for Religious.

As for the name of the Movement, Rita Di Maggio relates that at one of their early meetings, when the programme was being decided — in 1983 to be precise — it was mentioned that in Peru a group of ladies engaged in charitable apostolate had sprung up, called “Friends of Mother Rosa”. Asked whether that might also be the name of their Movement, Rita objected, maintaining that the name defines the path! Nevertheless, she agreed that the title “Friends of Mother Rosa” be adopted for the time being.

But in 1989, at a meeting with Mother Virginia, Rita Di Maggio again voiced her doubts about the name; the Mother invited her to pray and remain open to the Spirit. Later, on 24 May, during the celebration of the Eucharist, Mother Virginia had something like an illumination: “The name to give the Movement could be: ‘Movement of the Covenant or of Hope’.”

Accepting Mother Virginia's proposal, Rita Di Maggio immediately felt at ease and identified with the name “Movement of Hope”. Indeed, it reminded her of the image of the broken trunk from which a shoot sprang — the life of Mother Rosa broken and then blossoming again by grace. The very coat of arms of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne depicts this reality: “hoping against all hope!” (cf. Rom 4:18). And she felt: “yes, this name defines and illumines the spirituality of the Movement”.

Little by little the Movement of Hope made its way in the Church and in the world. Alongside every community of the Daughters of Saint Anne on the five continents, many lay people felt called to live the spirituality of the Institute in this form of life.

At the 18th General Chapter of the Daughters of Saint Anne, held in Rome from 3 December 1990 to 28 January 1991, Rita Di Maggio too was invited to give her testimony and describe the journey the Movement was making. With the definitive approval of the General Chapter and the subsequent authoritative confirmation by the Church in 1991, the Movement was fully called to share in and live in the world the Charism and spirituality of the Family of Saint Anne, founded by Blessed Mother A. Rosa Gattorno.

And in June 1992 the Statute was finally drawn up — the instrument to which the Movement constantly refers. It expresses the Movement's way of being in the Church, in the Charismatic Family and in the world. Called to live the same spirituality, the Statute of the Movement of Hope could only spring from the Basic Documents.

Every member of the Movement of Hope is called today to live in the world as a Sign of Hope, starting from their own lay condition, building a better world wherever they are, regardless of nation, culture or type of work. The Church has given a name to this wide field of action — the secular character of the lay vocation:

“What specifically characterises the laity is their secular nature […] By reason of their special vocation it belongs to the laity to seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and directing them according to God's will. They live in the world, that is, they are engaged in each and every work and business of the world and in the ordinary circumstances of social and family life which, as it were, form the context of their existence. There they are called by God to contribute to the sanctification of the world from within, like leaven, in the spirit of the Gospel, by fulfilling their own particular duties. Thus, especially by the witness of their life, resplendent in faith, hope and charity, they must manifest Christ to others. It pertains to them in a special way so to illuminate and order all temporal things with which they are so closely associated that these may be effected and grow according to Christ and may be to the glory of the Creator and Redeemer” (Lumen Gentium, 31).

After reading no. 31 of the Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium, reflection can be deepened with the following questions:

  1. In what way is living the Charism “in the world” not a limitation but the specific path of their sanctification?

  2. What aspects predominate in the way lay people today take part in living our Charism and mission?

  3. There is talk of a twofold responsibility: building the Church and sanctifying the world. Is there a balance between these two actions in the lives of our lay people?

With great trust let us address our prayer to God the Father, who calls every baptised person to be a builder of his Kingdom, and say together:

R. Grant that we may be faithful to our Baptism, O Lord.

  1. For all the lay faithful: that, aware of their Baptism, they may live their vocation with joy and responsibility, bringing the Gospel into the heart of families, workplaces, culture and society. Let us pray. R.

  2. For all the members of the Movement of Hope: that, in communion with the whole Family of Saint Anne, they may generously offer their gifts and talents for the growth of the Kingdom, being Signs of Hope. Let us pray. R.

  3. For their families: that, as “domestic churches”, they may be places of faith, love and welcome, supporting the human and spiritual growth of their children. Let us pray. R.

  4. For our Charismatic Family: that, faithful to our common Charism, we may always be united, reflecting the love of the Trinity and the joy of the Gospel. Let us pray. R.

Introduction

Arising as the male branch of the Charismatic Family, the Religious Institute of the Sons of Saint Anne marks the fulfilment of one of the great desires of Mother Rosa's heart: “Already I see the Sons of the heart of the Holy Mother Anne, all intent and full of the love of God […] Oh, blessed dream!” (Memoirs, p. 762).

Alongside her Daughters, as early as 1882, Mother Rosa dreamt of the Priests Sons of Saint Anne as “the finest of adornments”; and she saw them united not only in the same Charism but also in the same mission: for the increase of the holy faith, for works of charity and zeal, and for the consolation of the world.

In the Memoirs she refers several times to the plan concerning the “foundation”. And she would work for it with all her strength. But as it was then taking shape it did not seem to her to accord with God's will; and so, sustained by the certainty that at the right moment the hour would strike, she entrusted to Providence the carrying out of this singular design, which took a new and firmer start only some hundred years after her death.

So, for the Sons of Saint Anne too, the hour of rebirth seems at last to have come in 1991. And meanwhile the Spirit was calling, from many parts of the world, those whom he desired as “Sons of the heart of the Holy Mother Anne”.

“[I feel] always a strong urge to work for the Sons of Saint Anne. My God, what am I to do? I was thinking this because I can no longer find the draft of the Rules that I had and that had been inspired in me by my Good […] And an inner voice [says to me]:

Yes, I will, and you, my Good, guide the pen, prompt me, and then they will soon be written and with your most powerful help they will be observed. Oh, blessed dream! Moments of Paradise that make one forget everything, when only the desire that all be fulfilled reigns and fills the whole mind and allows no obstacles to appear!“

In the pages of her Memoirs Mother Rosa refers more than once to the plan for the “foundation of the Sons of Saint Anne” — an Institute of priests destined to work in the Church for the glory of God, the conversion of sinners, evangelisation and the formation of the Daughters of Saint Anne — and alludes to the inspiration she had received.

She speaks of this intuition for the first time: “I had never thought of the Sons of Saint Anne…” (Memoirs, p. 624). And she relates that, having met a learned and holy Franciscan in Naples, she was encouraged by him to pursue this plan. She writes in her intimate diary:

“So too [with] the matter of the foundation of the Sons of Saint Anne; he made me see so clearly that it was God's will that I should go to the Pope and tell him everything God had suggested to me, and not delay in obeying…; Oh my Love, what a second piercing! The first wound not yet healed, you want to open another; may your holy will be done in all things.” (Memoirs, p. 623).

There followed, however, years of uncertainty, fear and difficulty. In August 1884 she would write: “I expect great sorrows… certainly we shall have to fight… for me it is the most dreadful [thought] there can be, because the mere thought that I might do the least thing that is not his will…”. But the inner inspiration was confirmed to her several times by divine intervention:

“— Remember the three drops of my blood that I showed you and poured upon your heart; I told you that they will be the three Orders that you are to [found]”. (Memoirs, p. 665).

So she returned to the “planned foundation” during 1885. In June she wrote:

“[…] How my Good is preparing the Sons of Saint Anne is a great and extraordinary thing. I saw what was going on in a person who was to be the one to help me, but he is not generous [in answering] the call and he is afraid; so he will do [something] but not everything. What fear does!” (Memoirs, p. 715).

The person not named here, but easily identifiable, was Mgr Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, then secretary to Cardinal Guglielmo Sanfelice, Archbishop of Naples. He had known Mother Rosa since he was a seminarian, at the age of 23.

The fears the Mother mentions are more than understandable if one considers the social position and many commitments of Mgr di Belmonte. In August of the same year she again voiced her concern; nevertheless, she declared herself ready and willing to carry out God's plan humbly:

“The thought of the Sons of Saint Anne gives me great pain, because I fear it will happen to me as with the Daughters! […] a constant voice [whispers to me]:

— To work, and you will be consoled!

But how? [I am] alone, alone! My guide does not support me. Ah, my Good, have pity on me; I do not refuse, no, but I will always ask you for help, and you at least trace the way for me, and so I, ignorant as I am, will follow you. Oh my Love, I do not know what to do; send me help, for charity's sake, if you want this Work of the Sons of Saint Anne!“ (Memoirs, p. 730).

In 1886 the plan seemed to take clearer shape. Mgr Granito di Belmonte, after a pilgrimage to Rome and a powerful experience with Mother Rosa, convinced of the goodness of this inspiration and of God's will for this Work, decided to put it into effect. Received in private audience by Pope Leo XIII on 6 December of that year, he set out orally his intentions regarding the plan to found the Sons of Saint Anne. He was asked to put his ideas and the purpose of the new institution in writing, which he did two days later, entrusting the document to Mgr Nazareno Marzolini, a person very close to the Pope (draft of the petition in AFSA B.1.61).

“Most Holy Father, encouraged by the words of Your Holiness heard in the audience of 6 December of this month, Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte sets out on this sheet the ideas already humbly laid at the feet of Your Beatitude concerning the new Religious Family that he would wish to see created and blessed by Your Holiness. Some priests, now scattered in various Dioceses of Italy, would like to come together with the primary aim of undertaking the free care of the sick at home, especially clergy and the poor. They would take charge of hospitals and, in the cities to which they are called, besides caring for the sick and dying, they would teach catechism to children and preach, in the manner of spiritual exercises and missions, to the Daughters of Saint Anne nurses. This new Religious Family of nurses would serve under the special protection of Saint Anne, would have perfect common life with obedience to a major superior, and its principal house would be in Rome. The petitioner implores the Apostolic blessing upon the new Institute, which will be eternally grateful to Your Holiness for deigning to bless it at its beginning.” (Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. Rome, on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, 1886).

But after a series of vicissitudes, misunderstandings and misreadings, a new plan of foundation was conceived, and this troubled Mother Rosa not a little; she clearly expressed her bitterness and disagreement (cf. AFSA, various correspondence), which she also recorded in the pages of the Memoirs:

“The Work begun of the Sons of Saint Anne gives me great pain, because I see [it] is not as God desires it […] Oh, if only I could explain the wound I received when it was announced to me.” (Memoirs, p. 853).

The misunderstanding, however, was only temporary. The later letters between Mother Rosa and Mgr di Belmonte show no further second thoughts or disappointment, but rather an entrusting to the “protagonists of the future”:

“Dear Monsignor, you cannot believe what consolation your most dear letter brought me. Thank you! I have placed everything in God's hands and worry about nothing, because I am sure that the works of the Lord must begin like this […] Patience! I bear pain and sorrow over it, but what can be done? Wait for the hour of rebirth…” (Mother Rosa, 19 September 1887).

So in 1991 the hour of rebirth so long awaited by Mother Rosa seems at last to have come. With Vatican II's invitation to “return to the sources”, the Daughters of Saint Anne found themselves with her many writings, in which they discovered the unfinished chapter of the foundation of the “Sons of Saint Anne”.

After the historic date of the 18th General Chapter, as early as March 1991, the Daughters of Saint Anne welcomed a group of young men at their General House, organising a first experiential community of common life for a deeper knowledge of the Charism.

From the start there was growth in quality and in numbers among those responsible for formation. The experience gradually took concrete form in the Church of Rome and, with its natural development, by God's grace and abundant blessings, the Sons of Saint Anne were soon able to extend their presence to various Dioceses of the world, signifying not only the vitality of the Charism but also recalling them to the missionary and universal character of Mother Rosa's intuition.

On 8 December 2022 the Vicar of His Holiness for the Diocese of Rome, His Eminence Angelo Cardinal De Donatis, erected it as a Religious Institute of diocesan right, named Sons of Saint Anne, recognising Mother Rosa as its true Foundress. At present, besides Rome, the Institute is present in other parts of Italy and of the world: in Bolivia, Brazil, the USA, the Philippines, Kenya and Peru — and in some of these countries in several Dioceses.

“The servant of God did not seem to me convinced that she herself had to give up her plan [to found the Sons of Saint Anne], and she went on praying for this, hoping that in the future the Lord would hear her. “The Lord Jesus, «whom the Father has sent into the world» (Jn 10:36), has made his whole Mystical Body share in the anointing of the Spirit with which he himself was anointed. In him all the faithful are made a holy and royal priesthood […] The same Lord, however, has established ministers among his faithful to unite them together in one body in which «not all the members have the same function» (Rom 12:4). These ministers in the society of the faithful are able by the sacred power of Orders to offer sacrifice and to forgive sins, and they perform their priestly office publicly for men in the name of Christ. Therefore, having sent the apostles just as he himself had been sent by the Father, Christ, through the apostles themselves, made their successors, the bishops, sharers in his consecration and mission. The office of their ministry has been handed down, in a lesser degree indeed, to the priests. Introduction

Since 1986 a group of young women has been following a path of sanctification, proposing anew in “consecrated secularity” the spirituality proper to the Charismatic Family of Saint Anne. These Consecrated women, living secularity to the full — in their own families, alone or in small fraternities, practising a profession or a job that supports them — experience total abandonment into God's hands and trust in the Lord who guides history, so as to bear witness to the world of hope in the faithful God, the God for whom nothing is impossible. Their total Consecration to the Lord takes concrete form in the profession of the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, “lived in the world”. In this way the Consecrated women live an attitude that is “provocative” for our times, especially in the places where they live and work. Indeed, by remaining in the world and making themselves poor, weak, little, unarmed and vulnerable, the “Secular Daughters of Saint Anne” bear witness that power and glory belong to the living God. And by embodying poverty of heart, motherly dedication and the family spirit, they make visible in the world the features of the Mystery of Christ's Poverty, following the example of Mother Rosa, to whom God gave this Charism.

Commentary

Mother Rosa's life before founding the Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, as she tells it in her Memoirs, shows us a life devoted to charity but also to an intense spiritual relationship. This experience served as a point of reference for young women who felt called to live their vocation as Daughters of Saint Anne, but “immersed in the world”. It is true that in her time the form of Consecrated Life known as Secular Institutes had not yet arisen in the Church; this happened only in the mid-twentieth century with Pope Pius XII, who, welcoming this new reality in the Church, said in the motu proprio “Primo Feliciter” of 12 March 1948: “It must always be borne in mind that the proper and specific characteristic of these Institutes, namely their secularity, must be brought out in everything”. So it cannot be claimed that Mother Rosa had conceived this way of life in the Family of the Holy Mother at that time; yet in today's history the same Spirit has awakened in the hearts of many people the desire to live the Evangelical Counsels in a secular way of life, but according to her Charism and spirituality. Indeed, in 1986 a small group of lay women came into being in the Diocese of Crato – CE – Brazil. It was a small group whose members aspired to an ideal of Consecrated Life while remaining in their own situation. The first members were all former pupils of a school of the Daughters of Saint Anne, and among them one was also a former novice, who had left precisely with the ideal of beginning this experience. While still in the novitiate, Francisca Adália, after an experience of mission, felt in her heart a strong urge to put on the sentiments of Jesus, who, “when he saw the crowds, had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (cf. Mt 9:36). And as this call matured before the Blessed Sacrament, she understood that her vocation was precisely to live Mother Rosa's Charism, but in the world. Little by little the Spirit gave concrete form to this ideal of life in the gift of the Secular Institute. “Therefore the Institute recognises that its mission is born of Eucharistic contemplation” (cf. Constitutions of the FSA Secular Institute, art. 9 d). In the first months of the experience, a significant and providential presence was that of Mother A. Virginia Sinagra, then Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne. During her visit to the Communities of the Religious Province of Brazil-North she met Francisca Adália and the other members of this group. Listening to their aspirations, she offered her readiness to welcome God's manifestations and told her that in Italy too there was another person who had expressed the same desire to consecrate her life in a secular setting. The person Mother Virginia meant was Maria Raimondi, who had begun her experience as a lay woman in the “Movement of Hope” but had discovered that her vocation was to live “consecration in the world”. For some months, at Mother Virginia's suggestion, she too had begun to live an experience at Gregna, on the outskirts of Rome; there she lived and carried out her apostolate, while continuing her work as a leader of the groups of the Movement of Hope. Soon other lay women arrived too, who had long been waiting for a Secular Institute living the spirituality of the Family of Saint Anne: her sister Angelica, who had been widowed, Angela Fabbri, Pina Maccataio and Assuntina. Clearly all these events served to clarify ever more the identity of this group as well. Knowing of the existence of these two groups (one Brazilian and one Italian), Mother Virginia acted as a link between them, fostering communication and acquaintance. The relationship established by letter made it easier to share their experience, encouraging and supporting one another. These were two realities which, despite the distance, seemed alike in their essence: in the desire for consecration in secularity and the longing to live the same Charism and spirituality as the Daughters of Saint Anne. After this meeting Mother Virginia asked them to draw up a summary of their aspirations, to be presented to the Congregation for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life. In May 1988 the first consecration took place: Francisca Adália made her first profession in Brazil. This marked a fundamental step on their journey. From then on, requests began to come from people who found in this group the answer to their aspirations and wished to live a consecration in a Secular way of life. Only after the necessary time of formation, however, in 1996, did the first group, again in Brazil, make their first profession. As with the other expressions of the Charismatic Family, the welcome given by the 18th General Chapter of the Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne gave new impetus to the Secular Institute too. From then on the Mother General and her Council also took care of this “New Life”. In 1992 Francisca Adália was called to Italy by Mother Virginia with the specific purpose of drafting their Statute which, later translated into Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and English, made it easier for all candidates to come to know their reality. In early 1995 Mother Virginia submitted to the Vicar General of His Holiness, Cardinal Camillo Ruini, a request to “erect” canonically in the Diocese of Rome the Association of the Faithful preparatory to a female Secular Institute aggregated to the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne. On the very feast of the Presentation of the Lord, 2 February of that year, their Association was erected. Together with the decree of approval, Cardinal Ruini saw the need for an adequate period of time to make it possible to verify whether there were well-founded hopes for the survival and continuity of the experience, under the prudent and watchful care of the Episcopal Vicar for Consecrated Life, Fr Natalino Zagotto, who would follow the times and ways towards a future recognition and erection as a Secular Institute. Beyond spiritual communion, however, the way the Charism is lived, the style of life and the type of apostolate are completely different from those of a Religious Institute, being purely secular and lay. So, little by little, the Consecrated women discovered in practice that the Charism and the spirituality were the same, but the vocation was different. On 15 August 2003 the Vicar of His Holiness for the Diocese of Rome, His Eminence Camillo Cardinal Ruini, erected it as the Secular Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, also approving their Constitutions and recognising Francisca Adália Tavares de Oliveira as their Foundress, inspired by the Charism of Mother Rosa. At present the Institute is present in Italy, Bolivia, Brazil, the Philippines, Kenya and Peru.

Sharing

Secular Institutes correspond to a vision of the Church brought to the fore by the Second Vatican Council. Pope Paul VI said so authoritatively: “Secular Institutes must be seen in the perspective in which the Second Vatican Council presented the Church, as a living reality, visible and spiritual at once, which lives and develops in history” (cf. LG 8): “While secular institutes are not religious institutes, they nevertheless involve a true and complete profession of the evangelical counsels in the world, recognised by the Church. This profession confers a consecration on men and women, laity and clergy, who live in the world. Therefore they should make a total dedication of themselves to God in perfect charity their chief aim, and the institutes themselves should preserve their own special character, namely their secular character, to the end that they may be able to carry out effectively and everywhere the apostolate in the world and, as it were, from the world. Let them know, however, that they cannot accomplish so great a task unless their members are so thoroughly trained in matters divine and human that they will truly be a leaven in the world for the strengthening and increase of the Body of Christ. Superiors therefore should give serious attention to the formation, especially spiritual, of their subjects, and to developing it further.” (Perfectae Caritatis, 11).

After reading no. 11 of the Decree on the renewal of Religious Life, Perfectae Caritatis, reflection can be deepened with the following questions:

  2. Have I realised that the diversity of vocations in our Family is an added value? How can I contribute to unity?

  3. Do I feel that the family spirit is something that distinguishes us? How can I contribute to spreading this Charism and spirituality?

Introduction

Ever since the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council called for a renewal of Consecrated Life, a “return to the sources” has been necessary in order to identify and define, in the original inspiration of each Institute, the animating spirit (Charism) of this renewal.

The desire to define the existential meaning of our presence in the Church led the Religious Daughters of Saint Anne to study first of all what is regarded as an essential element received from Mother Rosa: the fact of being the “Family of the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate”:

“My Institute is nothing but an extension of my Family: God has raised you up so that in you, fortunate ones, we may go on living: I, your Mother; Joachim and Mary Immaculate” (Rule of 1869, ch. X, 1).

The Family of Saint Anne, arising in the Church as a manifestation of the manifold wisdom of God, lives its baptismal consecration in [various] particular forms of “sequela Christi” inspired by the Holy Mother of Mary, who, still alive and “present to the Lord” in the heavenly Homeland, continues to act through Him in her sons and daughters.

So, with this particular communion of life, shaped by the family spirit, they identify with Him in the “mystery of his poverty”, declaring themselves, like Mary, “servants of the Lord”, placed at the service of the poor in a Church of the poor (cf. Basic Doc., p. 5).

From the writings of Mother Rosa

(Memoirs, p. 320)

“In the [distance] I see many great things for our Institute; a light let me see the great panorama of the Order in the future. I will say that the divine [plan] was so beautiful and interwoven that I remained in ecstasy and rejoiced, while I saw in it a river of many sufferings. At that sight nothing frightened me; it seemed to me [that] I would [bear] as many again; but when I had calmly [come back to myself] and began to think, I was horrified. How will my ruined body hold out any longer? How shall I bear [the weight], so frail as I am, and how will my poor worn-out brain endure? On the other hand I turn my thoughts and say to myself:

— Have you not (also) seen that you are to be at the end of all this? You will have peace and tranquillity and you will die joyful in the Lord; why doubt?

[With] such reflections I feel strengthened, but if by chance I turn my mind away [from them] for an instant, I let myself be seized entirely by fear.”

From the Second Vatican Council to the present day, papal teaching and the Church's synodal journey have set before all the faithful the need and urgency of re-educating the sensus ecclesiae, that is, of faithfully rediscovering belonging to the Church as a mystery of communion, in all its truth and beauty. It has been no different for the Religious Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Rereading the “Basic Documents” and, consequently, our Constitutions and Statute, we are struck by how often the expressions “in the Church”, “with the Church”, “for the Church” and others like them appear… And this, we know, is the fruit and sign of the self-awareness that our Charismatic Family is fully part of the life of the Church, with its nature, its mission and its purpose.

There is no doubt that this self-awareness is the fruit of a deeper understanding of this mystery of communion in its Trinitarian, soteriological, ecclesial, charismatic, communal and missionary dimension. So this surprising newness did not imply any discontinuity or break with the tradition of the Religious Daughters of Saint Anne. On the contrary, as we have seen, there is truth in stressing that their Institute was born of obedience to the Church, and how much this sign has always shaped, historically and institutionally, the life of Mother Rosa and of the Institute.

So, in a grateful reading of our history, we know how the “Special Chapter” (1969-1971) was able to encourage all the good that the implementation of the Council brought with it, in abandoning institutional and pastoral patterns that had lingered on. And how much the “Basic Documents” set the tone for this renewal, in both charismatic and ecclesial understanding; and, further, that our recent Chapters and General Assemblies have taken up the Church's own proposal, setting in motion for us too the dynamic of a synodal journey.

But in this regard, speaking of appropriate renewal, we feel that we still need to combine those five essential aspects: a return to the sources, that is, to the Christ of the Gospel; a return to the spirit of the founders; communion in the life of the Church; knowledge of the modern world; inner renewal. These five aspects are in mutual tension and thus present a realistic view of the appropriate renewal desired by the Church.

And this opens up once more a wonderful horizon for our Charismatic Family, deeply rooted in the “mystery of Christ's poverty”. For with this Charism — which reveals in itself the centrality of the Christ of the Gospel — and with the values of fraternity, unity and communion, in the true family spirit that distinguishes us, we already manifest that idea of synodality which the universal Church is undertaking on this new path of renewal and revitalisation.

At the heart of this statement is also the awareness that the nature of our vocation is to “collaborate in the Church and with the Church in the saving work of Christ”. And, as we have seen, this is a particular trait of Mother Rosa's spirit: a call to be and to walk together with the whole Church for the transformation of the world into the new Kingdom of God.

It is therefore within this vision of our Charism and Spirituality, in some way already synodal, that our whole Charismatic Family, in the many forms in which it is expressed, finds its place. In our own way, we are already in tune with the main thrust of the Church's synodality, expressed as communion, participation and mission.

Underlying our approach to the Church's synodality, however, there must be a greater appreciation of the family spirit we are called to live ad intra, aware that this guarantees not only close collaboration among religious sisters and brothers, priests and lay people, but above all a concrete sign ad extra of unity and communion in a common Charism and spirituality.

In this sense, all the expressions of our Charism are called to conversion in the way they live this family spirit, and to be active, fully committed agents, not passive recipients. It is no longer the exclusive task of the Religious Daughters of Saint Anne to discern and safeguard the Charism; it is the task of all, equally and with the same passion. Above all, we are all called to embody it. We are all called to the same fidelity and co-responsibility, because we are all clothed with the same dignity of the “sublime vocation that has fallen to us” (cf. Rule of 1869, ch. I, 1). A new era of collaboration among the different expressions is therefore urgently needed, as the strength of a new time in the Church.

This awareness of ours, therefore, cannot and does not wish to be a reversal of roles, a substitution of responsibilities, still less a recruiting of labour to give the Charism more visibility, as other Religious Families have done in involving lay people above all in their mission (often for lack of vocations). Rather, it wishes to be a recognition that this is the most genuine expression of what we are meant to be as the Family of Saint Anne.

Essential on this path, then, is work done together, giving each person the opportunity to speak and be heard so as to contribute to building up this common good. And as Pope Francis recalled, the journey towards communion cannot consist in producing documents, but rather in “planting dreams, drawing forth prophecies and visions, allowing hope to flourish, inspiring trust, binding up wounds, weaving together relationships, awakening a dawn of hope, learning from one another and creating a bright resourcefulness that will enlighten minds, warm hearts, give strength to our hands” (cf. Address to the 15th Assembly of the Synod of Bishops).

And so, as we go forward and the Church's synodal style takes root in our Charismatic Family too, our “ancient yet ever new” way of placing the Charism at the service of the Church will become ever more incisive.

We do not, however, expect immediate change. Nor do we have all the answers in our pocket. We are working on it little by little. But it is clear that this new impetus must be centred on our unity and collaboration. We must all experience a new season of collaboration with one another, and especially with lay people.

To do this, what is needed is a correct vision of the Church and of our Family: that of the “People of God, of which every baptised person is fully a member”. Hence the invitation to “recover an integral ecclesiology”, which stresses unity and not separation into a kind of “ghetto” (cf. Pope Francis, 18/02/2023). But it is true that there is still a long way to go for the Church to live as one body, as a true People; and for us too, with the true “family spirit” so long dreamt of. In any case, it will always be God who shows the way to live in communion more intensely and more concretely.

We are certain that God will continue to bless our Charismatic Family with many women and men consecrated to his service as religious, priests and consecrated women. But we are equally certain that we must continue to be a help and an inspiration to all the lay men and women who wish to take up and live our Charism. We must therefore continue to support one another and to encourage new vocations.

“The Holy Spirit desires your multiformity and wants you for the one body, but in the concrete communion of the local Church, in true union with the successors of the Apostles and the Successor of Peter. In this way one works for the one body and in the unity of the one body […] The Holy Spirit blows where he wills. But his will is unity. He leads us towards Christ, into his body.” (Benedict XVI, 28/05/2006):

“Every renewal of the Church consists essentially in increased fidelity to her own vocation (U. R. 6) […] Our renewal, therefore, does not consist in doing something absolutely new, but in a deeper study of Mother Rosa's original inspiration and a clearer definition of the essential lines of her Charism, so as to give [our Family], with a new vital impulse, the possibility of fully embodying its vocation in the present historical moment. Unchanging fidelity to our origins, in the gradual adaptation of our spirituality to the changing conditions of places and times. The various documents of our origins show that Mother Rosa too only gradually discovered and understood the message of the Spirit concerning the specific character [her Charismatic Family] was to have.” (Basic Documents. Introduction, p. XXVII).

  3. How can we keep our Charism ever relevant without losing the original inspiration? And how can we spread it?
